bands.title: The first year: a foundation of trust
bands.lead: This year your baby learns whether the world is a safe place. The answer comes from your voice, your arms and the way you respond.
brain: In the first years of life, more than a million new neural connections form in the brain every second. Repeated everyday experience decides which pathways get stronger: your baby makes a sound, you answer; they cry, you come close.

The part of a baby’s brain that calms them down is still very immature. That is why your baby can’t settle on their own yet and “borrows” calm from your calm body. This is called co-regulation, and it is the very first lesson in self-regulation.

Around 6–9 months, memory and attachment grow stronger: your baby may start to be wary of strangers and get upset when you leave the room. This isn’t a step backwards — quite the opposite, it’s a sign they are attached to you.
needs: A response to their crying. At this age you can’t “spoil” a baby or get them “too used to being held”. Responding quickly and kindly teaches them to trust the world.
Face-to-face time: smiles, songs, copying their sounds. These “serve and return” games build the foundations of language and emotional development.
A predictable day: feeding, sleep and bath in roughly the same order. It’s not the exact clock time that matters, but a familiar rhythm.
Safe sleep and a safe environment — and a rested, supported parent.
normal: Long bouts of crying at certain times of day, especially in the late afternoon and evening, that seem to have no reason (in the first 3–4 months).
Waking often at night. Sleeping through the night in the first year is not the norm for every baby.
Putting everything in their mouth: this is how they explore the world.
Fear of strangers and crying when you’re not there (from around 8 months).
tryThis: A few times a day, 5 minutes of “face-to-face time”: phone away, copy your baby’s sounds, describe what they’re doing.
Talk your way through everyday tasks: “Now we’re changing your nappy. Legs up. All done!”
Play peekaboo: through this game your baby learns that “what goes away comes back”, and separation anxiety softens.
When the crying goes on and on and your patience runs out, put your baby down somewhere safe — in the cot — take a few minutes to breathe, then come back.
specialist: If your baby doesn’t react to sounds, doesn’t make eye contact with you, isn’t smiling by 4 months or doesn’t respond to their name by 9 months.
If they lose a skill they used to have (smiling, babbling, sitting).
If their crying is different from usual, or comes with fever, vomiting, unusual drowsiness or refusing feeds: see a doctor. If it’s serious, call {emergency}.
If you’ve felt sad, hopeless or afraid of harming your baby for weeks: this may be postnatal depression, and it can be treated. Tell your doctor.

bands.title: Ages 1–3: the “I do it myself!” stage
bands.lead: Your child is walking, starting to talk and wants to be independent — but the brain that manages feelings is still very young. That’s where tantrums come from.
brain: The brain’s emotion centre (the amygdala) is strong and fast, while the prefrontal cortex that “puts the brakes on” will keep developing for many years. That’s why a two-year-old can’t stop even when you say “stop”. It isn’t stubbornness — it’s brakes that aren’t finished yet.
Language develops fast, but what a child understands is far ahead of what they can say. Not being able to say what they want is hugely frustrating, and it often comes out as screaming or hitting.

At this age children learn cause and effect by experimenting: they drop the spoon, watch your reaction, drop it again. They’re not trying to wind you up — it’s a little scientist running an experiment.
needs: Calm, clear limits that stay the same: “No hitting. I’m holding your hands.” Not long explanations — a short sentence and action.
Choices: “Red T-shirt or blue?” Choice meets their need for autonomy and reduces the need to say “no”.
Naming their feelings: “You’re angry because the game is over.” A feeling that has a name settles faster.
A few minutes a day of play they lead, plenty of movement and fresh air.
normal: Several tantrums a day, especially when tired, hungry or at transition times.
Saying “No!” a lot and asking for the same thing over and over.
Not being able to share. Real sharing develops from around 3–4 years.
Occasional biting or hitting: physical aggression peaks at this age and then gradually declines.
tryThis: Give a 5-minute warning before transitions: “Two more goes on the slide, then we’re going home.”
Instead of “no”, say what they can do: “Not on the wall — draw on this paper.”
10 minutes a day of “their game”: whatever they do, you do too — no criticism, no barrage of questions.
Notice good behaviour during the day and name it precisely: “You gave the toy to your brother — look how happy he is!”
specialist: If there’s no pointing at 18 months, no two-word phrases at 2 years, no response to their name or very little eye contact.
If they lose words or skills they used to have (at any age).
If tantrums last longer than 25 minutes, happen more than 5 times a day, cause serious injury to themselves or others, or don’t ease off after age 4.
If sleep, eating or behaviour difficulties disrupt family life for months.

bands.title: Ages 3–6: imagination, questions and rules
bands.lead: Your child asks “why?”, sets up pretend play and learns about friendship. Self-control grows fast, but they still need your support.
brain: Executive functions — holding attention, waiting for a turn, remembering a rule, switching between ideas — develop rapidly between 3 and 5. Pretend play and games with rules are the best practice for these skills.
Your child begins to understand that other people can think differently. That’s why the first lies appear at this age — interestingly, a sign of cognitive development.
Imagination gets stronger and the line between real and made-up is still blurry. Fear of the dark, of monsters and of bad dreams are typical at this age.
needs: A few clear family rules, applied consistently. The more predictable the rules, the fewer the arguments.
Logical consequences, not punishment: “If you throw the ball indoors, the ball goes in the cupboard.”
Conversations about feelings: books, play with toys, questions like “how would you feel?”
Real little responsibilities: setting the table, tidying toys, watering a plant.
normal: Telling the occasional lie and mixing up fantasy and reality.
Testing rules and reacting strongly to “unfairness”.
Being afraid of the dark or of new situations.
Still having tantrums now and then, but shorter and less often than before.
tryThis: Once a day, ask “What was the best and the hardest moment of your day?” and really listen.
Draw the rules together in pictures and put them up on the wall.
Practise self-control with games like “Red light, green light” or “Simon says”.
When something goes wrong, find the fix together: “The water spilled. What shall we do?”
specialist: If at 4 they’re not making sentences, strangers find their speech hard to understand, or they show no interest in playmates.
If fears or anxiety disrupt daily life (nursery, sleep, eating) for weeks.
If aggression seriously hurts others or is getting worse; if there is cruelty to animals.
If after being dry for a long time they start wetting again during the day, or lose earlier skills.

bands.title: Ages 6–12: skills, friendship, self-confidence
bands.lead: The school years are when a child builds their sense of “I can do it”. Friends become important, but you are still their main anchor.
brain: Planning, attention and self-control are now well developed, but tiredness, hunger and stress easily “switch them off”. An irritable child after school is very often just a drained child.
Children start comparing themselves with others. In this period self-worth is fed mainly by effort, gaining skills and feeling accepted.
Closer to adolescence (around 9–12) hormonal changes may begin: mood swings and a greater need for personal space are normal.
needs: Encouragement that notices effort and strategy: “You worked really hard on this problem and tried another way.”
Gradually more responsibility and say in decisions, alongside clear family rules.
A parent who listens without judging. If you listen to the small things, they’ll tell you the big things too.
Free time beyond screens and homework: play, sport, friends, sleep.
normal: Long arguments about fairness and wanting to negotiate rules.
Falling out and making up with friends, and the hurt of “they wouldn’t let me play”.
Sometimes being embarrassed by their parents or wanting more time alone (especially after 10).
tryThis: A “no-interrogation chat” time in the car, at meals or before bed: tell them about your day too.
A fixed time and place for homework — but don’t do the homework for them.
Write a family screen plan together: where, when and how much.
Once a week, one-on-one time: just you and them, doing something they choose.
specialist: Sadness, loss of interest, or big changes in sleep or appetite lasting more than two weeks.
Persistent refusal to go to school, frequent complaints of tummy aches and headaches (when the doctor finds no cause).
Signs of being bullied or bullying others; complete withdrawal from friends.
Self-harm, or talk about death or suicide: never dismiss this as “attention-seeking”. Get professional help straight away, and if there is immediate danger call {emergency}.

articles.title: Tantrums: what’s happening in the brain?
articles.summary: A tantrum isn’t the result of bad parenting. It’s the moment a big feeling overwhelms a “braking system” that is still small.
science: The emotion system deep in the brain is powerful from birth: it registers danger, frustration and anger in an instant. The prefrontal cortex — the part that holds these feelings back and says “wait, there’s another way” — keeps maturing until around age 20. In 2–4-year-olds this gap is at its widest. That’s why, mid-tantrum, your child can’t hear you and doesn’t respond to reason: the “thinking” part of the brain is temporarily offline.

In that moment your child can’t calm down alone; they “borrow” calm from your body and your voice. Researchers call this co-regulation. The calmer the parent stays, the faster the child’s stress system returns to normal — and with repetition, the child learns and takes on this way of calming down. Shouting and punishing, on the other hand, raise stress hormones and make the tantrum last longer.

Tantrums tend to happen at the same moments: tiredness, hunger, transitions (from play to home, leaving the park), hearing “no”. Spotting these moments in advance can prevent more than half of tantrums.
tryToday: Calm yourself first: take one deep breath, drop your shoulders, lower your voice. If you’re not calm, they can’t be either.
Say little. One or two short sentences are enough: “You’re really angry. I’m here.”
Keep everyone safe: if they’re hitting, hold their hands gently, and move away anything they could hurt themselves with.
Once they’ve calmed down, cuddle them — and only then talk, briefly: “You got really angry because the game was over. Next time you can say ‘help me’.”
This week, note down when tantrums happen. Most likely they’ll line up with tired and hungry times.
mistakes: Giving long explanations or lectures during a tantrum. The brain isn’t in listening mode yet — calm first, talk later.
Giving in to stop the tantrum. That means a bigger tantrum next time. Show empathy for the feeling, but stick to your decision.
Shaming your child: “Shame on you, everyone’s looking at you.” Shame doesn’t teach them to manage feelings — only to hide them.
Seeing the tantrum as “manipulation”. For a young child it’s mostly a lack of skill, not a trick.

byAge.1-3: Their vocabulary is small, so you name the feeling and show a simple alternative: “You’re angry. Stamp your feet — like this!” Distraction works really well at this age.
byAge.3-6: In a calm moment, make an “anger plan” together: breathing, squeezing a cushion, going to a quiet corner. Put it on the wall in pictures, and when a tantrum starts, just point to it.

specialist: If tantrums regularly last longer than 25 minutes or happen more than five times a day.
If your child seriously hurts themselves during tantrums (head-banging, biting) or holds their breath until they pass out — see a doctor.
If after age 4–5 tantrums are increasing instead of easing off, or there are other concerns about speech, sleep or social interaction.

articles.title: Emotion coaching: naming feelings
articles.summary: Noticing and naming feelings strengthens a child’s self-control. It doesn’t mean allowing everything.
science: In the 1990s psychologist John Gottman observed families and found that parents respond to their children’s feelings in four different ways: dismissing (“Don’t cry, it’s nothing”), disapproving, laissez-faire (allowing everything) and “emotion coaching”. A coaching parent takes the feeling seriously, names it and looks for solutions together with the child — while still setting limits on behaviour.

Children of emotion-coaching parents went on to hold their attention better, have fewer conflicts with friends and recover from stress faster. Later programmes (for example, “Tuning in to Kids”) showed that any parent can learn this skill.
Brain research shows something interesting too: putting a feeling into words (“I’m angry”, “I’m scared”) reduces activity in the emotion centre. So “name it to tame it” is more than a nice phrase.
tryToday: Three times today, say your child’s feeling “as if” you were them: “Looks like you’re really disappointed.” Don’t worry if you get it wrong — they’ll correct you.
Allow the feeling, limit the behaviour: “It’s OK to be angry. It’s not OK to hit.”
When reading, look at the characters’ faces: “How do you think they’re feeling right now?”
Put your own feelings into calm words too: “I’m a bit tired, so I’m going to have a quiet cup of tea.” Your child copies you more than anyone.
mistakes: Saying “Don’t cry”, “There’s nothing to be scared of”, “It’s nothing”. The feeling doesn’t go away — your child just learns not to show it to you.
Thinking empathy cancels the “no”. You can absolutely say “I understand, you really wanted it. The answer is still no.”
Only talking about feelings in hard moments. The best practice happens in calm moments, through play and books.

byAge.1-3: Simple words: happy, angry, sad, scared. Copy facial expressions together in the mirror.
byAge.3-6: Draw a feelings “thermometer”: green — I’m calm, yellow — I’m getting upset, red — I’m going to explode. Let your child point to the colour.
byAge.6-12: Teach more nuanced words: disappointment, embarrassment, jealousy, worry. Ask where in their body they feel it.

specialist: If for a long time your child shows almost no feelings at all, or every little thing upsets them for hours.
If sadness, fear or anger lasts more than two weeks and affects sleep, eating, school and friendships — see a child psychologist.

articles.title: A calm-down corner and breathing games
articles.summary: You can teach a child to calm down — not with a naughty corner, but with a cosy place and games.
science: Self-regulation develops first together with a parent and then, gradually, on one’s own. The more times a child has calmed down alongside a calm adult, the better they learn the way.
Slow, deep breathing (especially a long out-breath) slows the heart rate and switches off the body’s “danger” mode. Children learn this better through play than through instructions.
tryToday: Set up a little “cosy corner” at home together: a cushion, a soft toy, a book or two, feelings cards. It isn’t a place of punishment — it’s somewhere they can go any time.
The “flower and candle” game: smell the flower (breathe in through the nose), blow out the candle (breathe out slowly through the mouth). Five times.
Practise together when things are calm: “What does our body feel like when we’re angry? Let’s practise breathing now, while we’re calm, so we remember when we need it.”
With a younger child, go to the corner together: “Come on, let’s go to the cosy corner together.”
mistakes: Using the corner as a punishment: “Go and stand in the corner!” Then your child will avoid going there.
Trying to teach breathing for the first time in the middle of a tantrum. Skills are learned in calm times.
Expecting calm “right now”. A big feeling can take 10–20 minutes to fade.

byAge.3-6: Putting a toy on their tummy and “rocking the toy with your breath” works really well.
byAge.6-12: Let your child write their own calm-down list: music, drawing, a walk, a drink of water. They’re more likely to use a method they chose themselves.

specialist: If your child almost never manages to calm down, or behaves dangerously when angry — see a child psychologist.

articles.title: Big feelings in school-age children
articles.summary: Anger, embarrassment, jealousy, disappointment: at school age feelings get more complex, and children need help understanding them.
science: By school age children can hide their feelings, so big feelings often explode at home — next to the safest person, you. Irritability after school is often the exhaustion of “holding it together” all day.
Social comparison begins at this age. Shame and an “I’m bad” feeling can look like anger. The better your child can name a feeling, the easier it becomes to manage.
tryToday: Don’t fire questions at them straight after school. Snack, quiet or a hug first — talk later.
Practise a “feeling + need” sentence together: “I feel … because … . I need … .”
Share a similar story from your own childhood: “When I was 9, I was embarrassed like that too…”
After a meltdown, go over it without blame: “What happened? What did you feel in your body? What would help next time?”
mistakes: Shrinking the feeling: “That’s not worth crying over.” For them, it’s big.
Jumping straight in with solutions. Sometimes a child just wants to be heard.
Treating anger as “unbecoming” in girls or sadness as “unbecoming” in boys. Every feeling is normal for every child.
specialist: Sadness, loss of interest, changes in sleep and appetite, or refusing school for more than two weeks.
Self-harm or talking about death: get professional help straight away, and if there is immediate danger call {emergency}.

articles.title: Whining and clinginess
articles.summary: Whining grates on your nerves, but it’s often a signal of tiredness or a need for attention.
science: Children quickly learn which behaviour works. If whining eventually gets them what they want, they’ll keep doing it. Attention — even negative attention — reinforces behaviour.
At the same time, whining is often a sign of hunger, tiredness or having gone a long time without attention. Responding to the cause quickly reduces the behaviour.
tryToday: In a calm moment, play the “strong voice” game: say the same request in a whiny voice and in a normal voice, and laugh together.
When they whine, say calmly: “I can hear you much better in your normal voice.” When they use their normal voice, respond straight away and with enthusiasm.
Get in first during the day: frequent, short attention for no reason — eye contact, a hug, “I see you”.
mistakes: Saying “no” first, then “fine, have it” when the whining drags on. Nothing teaches whining more powerfully.
Mocking the whining or imitating it to shame them.
specialist: If along with the whining your child often looks tired or pale, or has lost their appetite — see a doctor to check for medical causes.

articles.title: Positive discipline: limits and warmth together
articles.summary: The best outcomes come not from strict parents or from parents who allow everything, but from those who are both warm and clear.
science: In the 1960s psychologist Diana Baumrind described parenting styles along two dimensions: warmth (love, attention, responsiveness) and demands/structure (clear expectations, limits). The “authoritative” style, high in both, was linked with the best outcomes: more independent, more self-confident children with fewer behaviour problems.

In the decades that followed, meta-analyses combining hundreds of studies confirmed this: a warm relationship and limits set with explanation are associated with less aggression and rule-breaking, while harsh control and punishment are associated with more problem behaviour.

The American Academy of Pediatrics (2018) and the WHO (2022) recommend the same approach to parents: build a positive relationship, notice and reinforce good behaviour, set clear expectations and use calm consequences. Physical punishment and humiliating words are not recommended.
tryToday: Phrase one rule positively: not “Don’t run”, but “We walk indoors”.
State the expectation in advance: “In the shop you hold my hand, and we only put what’s on the list in the trolley.”
Today, notice good behaviour five times and name it precisely: “You hung up your bag yourself — thank you!” Whatever behaviour gets attention, grows.
Set the limit in a calm, short, kind voice, then follow through. No repeated warnings.
mistakes: Setting love and limits against each other. “I love you, and that’s why I’m not allowing it” — both can go together.
Enforcing a rule one day and forgetting it the next. Consistency matters more than strictness.
Only reacting to mistakes. If problem behaviour is the only way your child gets attention, they’ll repeat it.

byAge.1-3: Environment more than words: put dangerous things out of reach and save “no” for what really matters.
byAge.3-6: 3–4 simple family rules are enough. Draw them in pictures and put them somewhere visible.
byAge.6-12: Discuss rules together and agree on consequences in advance. When a child writes part of a rule themselves, they follow it more.

specialist: If, despite all your efforts, behaviour problems disrupt family life, nursery or school for months — a child psychologist or parenting programmes (for example, PCIT, Triple P) are very effective.

articles.title: Why hitting doesn’t work — and what does
articles.summary: A smack may bring instant obedience, but it makes behaviour worse in the long run. The scientific evidence on this is very clear.
science: In 2016 Gershoff and Grogan-Kaylor combined 75 studies covering more than 160,000 children. The result: spanking is not linked with a single positive long-term outcome — on the contrary, it’s associated with more aggression, antisocial behaviour, mental health problems and a weaker relationship with the parent. The link shows up even with “light” smacking or smacking “out of love”.

The reason is simple: hitting doesn’t teach a child what to do, it only teaches fear. It also shows that problems are solved by force. Shouting, threats and humiliation have a similar effect: in research, harsh verbal discipline has been linked with more behaviour problems and depressive symptoms in later years.

The American Academy of Pediatrics (2018) and the WHO do not recommend physical punishment or humiliating words. What works instead: a warm relationship, clear rules, reinforcing good behaviour, logical consequences and time to calm down.
tryToday: Choose a “stop signal” for yourself: when your temper rises, put your hands in your pockets, or take a step back and count to 10.
Stop dangerous behaviour physically but without harm: hold their hand, pick your child up, take the object away.
Teach what to do next time: “When your brother takes your toy, you can say ‘give it back!’ — or come to me.”
If you’ve already hit: apologise, take responsibility for your own behaviour and say what your plan is. This also teaches your child how to recover from a mistake.
mistakes: Thinking “I was smacked and I turned out fine”. Many people did turn out well regardless, but research shows that on average the risk goes up.
Keeping hitting as a “last resort”. The real last resort is taking a break to calm down and asking for help.
Replacing physical punishment with another humiliating method (shaming, threats, withdrawing love).

byAge.1-3: The most effective methods at this age: distraction, changing the environment, calmly moving your child away from danger.
byAge.3-6: Logical consequences and “time-in” (calming down next to you) work well.
byAge.6-12: Briefly limiting a privilege (for example, screen time) and solving the problem together.

specialist: If you feel you can’t control yourself when you’re angry, or that you might hurt your child — that’s a strong reason to ask for help. A psychologist or a parenting programme can change things.
If your child or you are in danger, or there is violence at home, call {emergency} immediately.

articles.title: Consequences vs punishment: what’s the difference?
articles.summary: Punishment aims to hurt; a consequence aims to teach. The best consequence is related to the behaviour, respectful and known in advance.
science: Behavioural psychology shows that what changes behaviour most is what follows it. But punishments (hitting, humiliating, long deprivations) create fear and resentment, and the child starts thinking about “how not to get caught”.

A logical consequence, on the other hand, is directly linked to the behaviour, short, and it teaches: drew on the wall with paints — we clean it together; broke the bike rule — no bike today. Natural consequences (went out without a jacket — got cold) are the most powerful teacher, as long as they are safe.
tryToday: The “3 R” check: is the consequence Related to the behaviour, Respectful and Reasonable?
Say the consequence in advance: “If you don’t tidy the toys, tomorrow they’ll have a rest in the box.” Then follow through calmly.
Keep the consequence short: one day is enough. A month-long ban doesn’t teach more — it just hurts.
After the consequence, a “clean slate”: no lecture, we start again.
mistakes: Making up consequences while angry: “No bike for a year!” Then you can’t carry it out and your word loses its value.
A punishment unrelated to the behaviour: didn’t do homework — can’t go to the birthday party.
Applying a consequence with sarcasm or an “I told you so”.

byAge.3-6: The consequence has to be immediate and very short. Hours later, your child won’t connect it with the behaviour.
byAge.6-12: Decide the consequences together. Children follow rules they think are fair much more.

specialist: If no consequence works and the behaviour is dangerous or strong enough to exhaust the family — talk to a child psychologist and look into parenting programmes.

articles.title: How to talk without shouting
articles.summary: Shouting brings instant relief, but your child gets used to the volume and hears you less. Speaking calmly and up close is more powerful.
science: In research, discipline with regular shouting, swearing and humiliating words has been linked with more behaviour problems and depressive symptoms in later years — even when the relationship is generally warm. One reason: shouting switches on the child’s stress system, and instead of listening they go on the defensive.
The good news: a parent’s self-regulation is a skill that can be learned. Shouting is very often a signal of the parent’s tiredness, hunger and overload — not of being a “bad parent”.
tryToday: Instead of shouting from across the room, come close, get down to your child’s level, make eye contact, say their name and speak in a short sentence.
When you want to raise your voice, do the opposite: whisper. Children listen to a whisper with curiosity.
Note the moments you shout during the day. What time is it most often? Make a plan for that time (for example, a snack, preparing things in advance).
If you shout, repair it: “I shouted, and that wasn’t OK. I was upset, but I shouldn’t have raised my voice.”
mistakes: Beating yourself up after every slip. That only creates more tension next time. The goal isn’t perfection, but shouting less often and repairing.
Saying “You make me shout”. We are responsible for our own feelings.
specialist: If anger and irritability get out of control almost every day, or come with sleeplessness, sadness or hopelessness — talk to a doctor or psychologist. Parental depression and anxiety can be treated.

articles.title: Time-out or time-in?
articles.summary: A short calm-down break can work, but what young children mainly need isn’t isolation — it’s closeness that helps them calm down.
science: The classic “time-out” (a calm break of a few minutes) has been studied within some parenting programmes, and when used correctly (short, calm, without humiliation, within a warm relationship) it has been shown not to be harmful. But it doesn’t mean locking a child in a room or frightening them.

“Time-in” means your child calms down next to you. It’s a better fit for young children, because they still need co-regulation. Either way, the goal isn’t punishment but calming down and “starting again”.
tryToday: Rule of thumb: about one minute per year of age, 5 minutes at most.
The place should be quiet, but not scary. Never lock a child in a dark room.
For time-in: “Come and sit next to me. Let’s breathe together.”
After the break, a short “let’s start again” — no lecture.
mistakes: Using time-out for long periods, often and with threats.
Combining the break with humiliation: “Go away, I don’t want to see you.”
specialist: If your child experiences terrible fear or panic during every break, or moments of separation overwhelm them — talk to a specialist.

articles.title: Family rules: few, clear, consistent
articles.summary: Children test limits because they want to know whether they’re still there. A steady limit gives a sense of safety.
science: A predictable environment calms a child’s stress system. In research, clear rules and a daily routine are linked with better sleep, fewer behaviour problems and stronger self-control.
The rules that work best are few (3–5), written in positive language and applied the same way by both parents.
tryToday: Hold a family meeting: everyone suggests one rule, and together you choose 3–5 main rules.
Write the rules positively: “Gentle hands”, “We listen to each other when someone is talking”, “Plates go to the kitchen after meals”.
Agree on consequences alongside the rules.
Adults follow the rules too. Children watch your example more than your words.
mistakes: Inventing a new rule for every new problem. Too many rules is the same as no rules.
One rule with mum, another with dad or grandma. The adults need to agree among themselves first.
specialist: If there are constant, tense conflicts about rules in the family, a family counsellor can help.

articles.title: The child who says “No!”: dealing with stubbornness
articles.summary: The “no” stage is your child discovering “I’m a separate person”. Fighting it doesn’t work — giving choices does.
science: In their second year children discover that they have a will of their own. The need for autonomy is one of the basic psychological needs: the more sense of control a child gets, the more ready they are to cooperate.
Research shows that “controlling” language (“Get dressed right now!”) increases resistance, while choices and explanations increase cooperation.
tryToday: Offer two acceptable choices: “Teeth first, or pyjamas?”
Use a statement instead of a yes/no question: “Now it’s time to get dressed” — not “Shall we get dressed?”
Turn it into a game: “Let’s see who can put their socks on faster — you or the teddy?”
Let go of battles that don’t matter: if the T-shirt is on back to front, the world won’t end.
mistakes: Turning every “no” into a power struggle.
Offering a choice and then not accepting what your child chose.
specialist: If your child responds to almost no requests, doesn’t react to their name or finds it hard to connect with others — see a doctor for a developmental check.

articles.title: Attachment: your child’s safe harbour
articles.summary: Secure attachment doesn’t come from perfect parenting, but from “good enough”, sensitive and reliable parenting.
science: John Bowlby described attachment as a child’s instinct to seek closeness when in danger. Mary Ainsworth observed that children whose parents were sensitive and predictable used them as a “secure base”: they explored freely, and when frightened they came back and calmed down.

Secure attachment is linked in later years with better emotional regulation, friendship skills and self-confidence. Importantly, this doesn’t require responding instantly and perfectly to every cry. Research shows that a large part of interaction consists of “mismatched” moments — what matters is repairing them afterwards.

Attachment isn’t built once and done: at school age too, your child needs to know they can come back to you in hard moments. It’s just that now it happens less through cuddles and more through listening and a sense of “I’m on your side”.
tryToday: When your child comes to you (happy or sad), give them your full attention for a few seconds: put the phone down, look them in the eye.
Create a short goodbye ritual that’s always the same: a hug, “see you this evening” — and then really go. Sneaking out damages trust.
Once a day, join in with their interests: whatever they’re playing, whatever they’re talking about.
Repair a moment when you lost your temper: “I was impatient this morning. Let’s start again.”
mistakes: Leaving a baby to cry for fear they’ll “get used to being held”. In the early months, responding doesn’t reduce independence — it increases it.
Thinking attachment means “never leaving your child”. Children form secure bonds with grandparents, the other parent and carers too — and that’s a good thing.
Trying to be perfect. Your child doesn’t need an ideal parent, but a genuine one who can repair.

byAge.0-1: Respond to crying, make eye contact, talk, sing. There’s no such thing as spoiling at this age.
byAge.1-3: Your child explores and comes back. Sitting in the park and saying “I’m here” is enough.
byAge.3-6: 10–15 minutes of special playtime a day strengthens attachment.
byAge.6-12: Listen without judging. If you’re there for their small problems, they’ll bring you their big ones too.

specialist: If your baby avoids eye contact, shows no interest in you or familiar people, or is almost impossible to soothe — see a doctor.
If your child attaches to everyone, even strangers, equally and indiscriminately (especially after difficult early years) — see a child psychologist.

articles.title: When your baby cries: the “you’ll spoil them” myth
articles.summary: Crying is your baby’s only language. Responding doesn’t create a spoiled child — it creates trust.
science: The American Academy of Pediatrics says it plainly: you can’t spoil a baby in the first months. Responding kindly to crying calms the baby’s stress system and builds the belief that “the world is safe”.

At the same time, it’s normal for healthy babies to cry a lot in the first weeks: crying starts increasing at around 2 weeks, peaks at 6–8 weeks and eases off by 3–4 months. Sometimes there’s no cause to be found. That isn’t your failure.

The most important safety rule: when you reach your limit, never shake your baby. Shaking can cause brain injury. Putting your baby down on their back in the cot and leaving the room for a few minutes is absolutely the right thing to do.
tryToday: Check the basics: hunger, nappy, too hot or too cold, wind, tiredness.
Try soothing techniques: swaddling (with hips free), rhythmic rocking, a “shhh” sound, walking around holding them, skin-to-skin contact.
Make a backup plan for the crying hours: take turns with your partner, a grandparent or a neighbour.
If your patience is running out: put your baby down somewhere safe, breathe for 5–10 minutes, drink some water, call someone, then come back.
mistakes: Leaving a very young baby alone for a long time because “if you let them cry, they’ll get used to it”.
Blaming lots of crying on your own “bad parenting”. This phase passes.
Being embarrassed to ask for help.
specialist: If the crying comes with fever (especially in a baby under 3 months), vomiting, diarrhoea, refusing feeds, unusual drowsiness or an unusual high-pitched cry — see a doctor straight away. If it’s serious, call {emergency}.
If you find yourself thinking about shaking or harming your baby, ask for help immediately. It doesn’t make you a bad person — it shows your exhaustion has reached its limit.

articles.title: 10 minutes a day: special time
articles.summary: A short daily playtime led by your child is one of the most powerful tools for reducing behaviour problems.
science: The first stage of PCIT (Parent–Child Interaction Therapy), one of the most researched parenting programmes, is built on exactly this: 5–10 minutes a day of play led by the child, while the parent praises, describes and imitates. Meta-analyses show these programmes significantly reduce behaviour problems.
The reason is simple: when a child’s need for attention is met in a positive way, they have less need to “earn” attention through negative behaviour.
tryToday: Set a timer: 10 minutes. Phone in another room.
Your child chooses the game, you follow. No commands, no barrage of questions, no criticism.
Describe what they’re doing: “You put the red block on the very top.” Copy them, praise them: “You’re building so carefully!”
When you finish, say: “I really loved playing with you. Again tomorrow.”
mistakes: Cancelling special time because of bad behaviour. It isn’t a punishment or a reward — it’s a daily vitamin.
Turning play into a “lesson”: “What colour is this? How many blocks are there?”

byAge.1-3: 5 minutes is enough. Sit on the floor, at their level.
byAge.6-12: Give it a name: “mum-and-son time”. It could be a card game, cooking together or a walk.

specialist: If special time and other strategies bring no change at all after a few weeks, or behaviour problems are severe — see a specialist about PCIT or similar programmes.

articles.title: Separation anxiety and settling into nursery
articles.summary: Crying at separation is a sign of attachment. A short, warm goodbye and a predictable return make settling in easier.
science: Separation anxiety starts at around 8–10 months, peaks at 15–18 months and usually eases towards age 3. It’s the period when a child doesn’t yet fully understand that the parent hasn’t “disappeared”.
What increases a child’s anxiety most is unpredictability. Sneaking away may reduce tears in the moment, but in the long run it makes the child cling more.
tryToday: Create a short goodbye ritual that’s always the same: a hug, a kiss, “I’ll come after lunch” — then go.
Before starting nursery, do short practice separations: 15 minutes, then 1 hour.
Link your return to an event your child understands: “I’ll come after your nap, after snack time.”
A “transition object” from home — a small toy, a photo of you — can comfort them.
mistakes: Not being able to leave a crying child, turning back at the door again and again.
Laughing at your child’s fear or saying “you’re a big kid, it’s embarrassing”.
specialist: If separation anxiety is much stronger than expected for their age, disrupts sleep, eating and going to nursery for weeks, or has started again at school age — see a child psychologist.

articles.title: Bedtime routine: the same three steps every evening
articles.summary: A simple routine repeated every evening helps your child fall asleep faster and wake less at night.
science: In a randomised study (Mindell and colleagues, 2009), a 3-step bedtime routine — bath, massage or lotion, a quiet activity (cuddles, a lullaby) — led to children falling asleep faster and waking less at night in just two weeks, and mothers’ mood improved too. Later reviews showed that bedtime routines are also linked with language development and emotional regulation.

Recommended sleep by age (including naps): 4–12 months — 12–16 hours, 1–2 years — 11–14 hours, 3–5 years — 10–13 hours, 6–12 years — 9–12 hours. In children, lack of sleep often shows up not as tiredness, but as irritability and hyperactivity.
Safe sleep rules matter for babies: on their back, on a firm, flat mattress, with no pillows or duvets, ideally in the same room as the parent but in their own bed.
tryToday: Start a routine from this evening: for example, bath → pyjamas and teeth → book and lullaby. The same order every evening, at about the same time.
Turn off screens and dim the lights an hour before the routine.
Make a picture chart of the routine together, and let your child “tick off” each step themselves.
Keep the routine to no more than 20–30 minutes. The longer it gets, the more your child will try to stretch it.
mistakes: A different time and a different order every evening. The brain is looking for predictable cues.
Exciting play, screens or shouting before bed.
Treating sleep methods as “mandatory”. Sitting beside them, not co-sleeping, gradually moving further away — choose what suits your family. No single method is essential for everyone.

byAge.0-1: Keep the routine short: bath, feed, lullaby. You can try putting your baby down drowsy but awake — and don’t worry if it doesn’t work.
byAge.1-3: Offer a choice: “Shall we read this book or that one?” Bedtime isn’t up for negotiation — the book is.
byAge.3-6: The questions to “stretch out” bedtime begin. Build a “last question” or “last cuddle” moment into the routine.
byAge.6-12: Keep phones, tablets and TV out of the bedroom. Plan bedtime together, alongside homework and sport.

specialist: If your child snores, has pauses in breathing or breathes through their mouth while asleep, and is very sleepy during the day — see a doctor.
If sleep problems last more than a few weeks and seriously disrupt family life.

articles.title: Night waking and night fears
articles.summary: Nightmares and night terrors are different things. Each needs a different approach.
science: Nightmares happen in the second half of the night, during dreaming (REM) sleep. Your child wakes up, says they’re scared, recognises you and needs comfort.

Night terrors (pavor nocturnus), on the other hand, usually happen 1–3 hours after falling asleep, in deep sleep. Your child may scream and have their eyes open, but they aren’t actually awake, don’t recognise you and remember nothing in the morning. They are common between ages 3 and 7 and are usually harmless.
tryToday: After a nightmare: cuddle, comfort briefly, turn the light up a little. Don’t make them tell you all the details at night — talk about it tomorrow.
During a night terror: don’t try to wake your child, just keep them safe and stay calmly nearby. Once the episode passes, they’ll carry on sleeping.
Lack of sleep makes night terrors more likely: try moving bedtime 20–30 minutes earlier.
During the day, talk about fears through play: draw a “monster book” together and make the monsters funny.
mistakes: Shaking your child awake during a night terror.
Mocking the fear: “There’s no such thing as monsters, don’t be silly.”
specialist: If episodes happen very often (several times a week), last longer than 30 minutes, involve unusual movements (rhythmic jerking, wetting) or cause daytime sleepiness — see a doctor.

articles.title: Picky eating: who’s responsible for what?
articles.summary: The parent decides what, when and where food is eaten; the child decides how much, and whether to eat at all. This division ends food battles.
science: Wariness of new foods (neophobia) is very common between ages 2 and 6 and makes evolutionary sense: it protects a young child from unknown, potentially dangerous food. It’s usually a passing phase.

Research shows that forcing a child to eat, saying “just one more spoonful” and rewarding with sweets all backfire: they increase dislike of that food and weaken the child’s ability to hear their own hunger and fullness signals. Instead, repeated offering without pressure — often 10–15 times — increases acceptance.
Dietitian Ellyn Satter’s “division of responsibility” model turns this evidence into a practical rule: the parent chooses the menu, the time and the place; the child chooses how much to eat.
tryToday: At every meal, include at least one “safe” food your child likes, plus a small piece of a new food alongside.
Put the new food out without comment. If they don’t eat it, say nothing. Try again tomorrow, and the day after.
Eat together as a family, without screens. Your child needs to see you eating with enjoyment.
Get your child involved in the kitchen: washing vegetables, mixing a salad. Children taste more of what they’ve made themselves.
Set times for meals and snacks, with no “grazing” in between.
mistakes: Forcing, bribing (“eat your broccoli and you’ll get chocolate”) or punishing.
Cooking a separate “restaurant menu” for your child at every meal.
Insisting on a clean plate. Your child needs to be able to hear their own feeling of fullness.

byAge.1-3: Finger foods, small portions, letting them feed themselves. Getting messy is part of learning.
byAge.3-6: A “tasting rule”: tasting isn’t compulsory, but looking at, smelling and touching a new food can be a game.
byAge.6-12: Involve them in menu planning: once a week, let them choose a new vegetable.

specialist: If your child is losing weight, falling behind on the growth chart, accepts very few foods (for example, fewer than 15), or gags, chokes or feels pain while eating — see a doctor.
If there is strong panic around food, vomiting or complete refusal of certain textures — a feeding specialist can help.

articles.title: Screen time: a smart plan for every age
articles.summary: At a young age, screens can’t replace real interaction. As children grow, the goal isn’t a ban but a family plan built together.
science: Young children learn very little from screens compared with a live person: language and social skills are built in face-to-face “serve and return” interaction. Even a TV on in the background reduces how much the parent talks with the child.

WHO (2019): screen time is not recommended for children under 1; at ages 2–4 it should be no more than 1 hour a day — less is better. American Academy of Pediatrics (2016): avoid screens (except video calls) until 18 months; at ages 2–5, up to 1 hour a day of high-quality content, watched with a parent whenever possible; from age 6, consistent rules that don’t get in the way of sleep, physical activity and social time.
Screens before bed delay falling asleep. Screens at mealtimes weaken a child’s ability to notice when they’re full.
tryToday: Set screen-free zones: the dinner table and the bedroom.
Turn screens off an hour before bed.
Give advance warning that screen time is ending and use a timer: “When the timer goes off, the tablet goes for a rest.”
Watch something together once and talk about it: “Why do you think she did that?” This turns screen time into connection.
Keep an eye on your own phone too: turn off notifications when your child is with you.
mistakes: Making the screen your main tool for stopping tantrums. Your child doesn’t learn to calm down.
Setting rules only for your child. Children copy their parents’ screen habits.
Seeing all screens as “bad”. Video calls, educational content watched together and creative apps are different.

byAge.0-1: No screens, except video calls. Your baby’s best “screen” is your face.
byAge.1-3: As little as possible until age 2. If they watch, keep it short, slow-paced and with you.
byAge.3-6: Up to 1 hour a day of high-quality, ad-free content. Not at meals and not before bed.
byAge.6-12: Write a family media plan together: homework, sleep, sport and friends come first. Respect the age limits for social media accounts.

specialist: If your child becomes extremely aggressive when the screen is taken away, shows no interest in anything else, or their sleep and schoolwork are seriously disrupted — see a child psychologist.

articles.title: Potty training: no rush
articles.summary: The most important step in potty training is waiting for signs of readiness. Most children are ready between ages 2 and 3.
science: In the 1960s paediatrician T. Berry Brazelton proposed a “child-oriented” approach: start when the child shows signs of readiness, without pressure or punishment. This approach is still the basis of the American Academy of Pediatrics’ recommendations today.

Signs of readiness: staying dry for 2 hours or more, being bothered by a wet nappy, understanding simple instructions, being able to pull trousers up and down, showing interest in the toilet. Night-time dryness comes later: wetting at night is normal until age 5–6.
tryToday: Check for signs of readiness. If they’re not there yet, wait — that’s normal.
Let your child choose the potty or toilet seat. At first, they can sit on it fully dressed and read a book.
After meals and naps, have a short “potty time”, and say thank you whatever the result.
Meet accidents calmly: “It happens. Come on, let’s clean up together.”
mistakes: Punishing, shaming or comparing with other children. This can lead to constipation and fear of the toilet.
Starting during big changes (a new baby, moving house, starting nursery).
Making them sit for a long time.

byAge.1-3: Play “potty” with toys and read books about it. Don’t rush to start.
byAge.3-6: Accidents are normal, especially when they’re absorbed in play. It’s fine to keep a night-time nappy for now.

specialist: Painful or very infrequent bowel movements (constipation), pain or burning when weeing, frequent daytime accidents after age 4.
If daytime or night-time wetting starts again after a long time of being dry — see a doctor.

articles.title: The morning rush: getting out without shouting
articles.summary: Most morning conflicts are solved the evening before. Preparation, a picture plan and a little spare time work wonders.
science: In rushed, tense moments, the executive functions of both parent and child — planning, remembering, patience — get weaker. That’s why morning rules work better as a chart you can see than as words.
Routines that give a child a sense of control (steps they tick off themselves) increase cooperation and reduce the need for repeated reminders.
tryToday: Get clothes, bag and shoes ready the evening before. Let your child choose their own clothes.
Make picture cards for the morning steps: get up → toilet → get dressed → breakfast → teeth → shoes.
Build in 15 minutes of spare time: write down an earlier leaving time for yourself.
Keep mornings screen-free, at least until everyone is ready.
mistakes: Repeating the same thing dozens of times. Say it once, then point to the card.
Doing everything for your child because “it’s quicker that way”.
specialist: If your child complains of tummy aches or headaches every morning, or persistently refuses to go to nursery or school — talk to a doctor or psychologist.

articles.title: “Serve and return”: the secret of language and the brain
articles.summary: Your child “serves” a signal — a look, a sound, a gesture — and you “return” it. This simple game builds the architecture of the brain.
science: Harvard University’s Center on the Developing Child compares this back-and-forth interaction to a game of tennis: the baby makes a sound, looks, points; the adult responds. As this “serve and return” is repeated, the neural pathways for language, attention and social skills grow stronger. Being left without a response, on the other hand, causes stress.

One fascinating study (Romeo and colleagues, 2018) showed that activity in the language areas of a child’s brain is better explained not by the number of words they hear, but by the number of conversational turns. In other words, what matters isn’t talking a lot — it’s talking with them.
tryToday: Notice where your child’s attention goes and put it into words: “Yes, a dog! A big brown dog.”
Wait for an answer: staying quiet for 5 seconds after a question gives your child time to take their turn.
Copy your baby’s sounds and stretch them a little: they say “ba”, you say “ba-ba-ball!”
Narrate everyday tasks like a “sports commentator”: “I’m washing the potatoes, now I’m cutting them…”
mistakes: Turning talking into a “lesson”: “Say ‘apple’! Say ‘apple’!” Pressure reduces speech.
Correcting your child’s words straight away. Instead, simply repeat the correct form: “Nana? Yes, a yellow, soft banana.”
Looking at your phone when you’re with your child. Every notification is a “ball that doesn’t come back”.

byAge.0-1: Face to face: smile, sing, respond to your baby’s sounds.
byAge.1-3: Name the things your child points to, ask simple questions, stretch one word into two.
byAge.3-6: Explore “why?” questions together and ask open questions: “What do you think will happen next?”

specialist: If there are no gestures (waving, pointing) at 12 months, no words at 16–18 months, or no two-word phrases at 2 years — see a doctor or a speech and language therapist.
If at any age your child has lost words they used to say — don’t wait, see a doctor.

articles.title: The power of play: why play isn’t “wasted time”
articles.summary: Free play strengthens a child’s executive functions, creativity and resilience to stress.
science: The American Academy of Pediatrics’ 2018 report (“The Power of Play”) calls play not a “luxury” but a necessity for child development. In play, children plan, keep to rules, negotiate with others and learn to tolerate frustration.
Pretend play (“shop”, “doctor”) is especially good practice for executive functions: the child has to stay in role, remember the rules and hold back their own impulses.
tryToday: Keep at least an hour a day for unstructured play (it can be split up, depending on age).
Choose simple, open-ended toys: blocks, boxes, paints, dressing-up clothes. Fewer toys mean more creativity.
Once a week, free play outdoors: trees, sand, water, sticks.
Sometimes join the game in a “wrong” role: you’re the customer, they’re the shopkeeper.
mistakes: Filling every minute with clubs and activities. Boredom is where creativity begins.
Always winning or always losing in games. Your child needs to learn both.
specialist: If after age 2–3 your child still shows no interest at all in pretend play, their play is very repetitive and unchanging, or they have no interest in playing with other children — see a doctor for a developmental check.

articles.title: Reading together: from day one
articles.summary: Reading books together from babyhood is one of the simplest and most powerful habits for language, attention and attachment.
science: The American Academy of Pediatrics (2014) advises paediatricians to encourage parents at every check-up to read with their children from infancy. Reading together builds vocabulary, listening skills and later reading success.

The biggest benefit comes from “dialogic reading”: the parent asks questions, expands on the child’s answers and talks about the pictures. In other words, a book is also a tool for “serve and return”.
tryToday: 10–15 minutes of reading together a day, ideally as part of the bedtime routine.
Ask one question on every page: “What do you think the cat will do now?”
If your child wants the same book 20 times — read it. Repetition is one way of learning.
At school age, take turns reading: one page you, one page them.
mistakes: Presenting reading as a compulsory lesson.
Stopping reading aloud once your child starts reading on their own. Reading aloud is beneficial right up to age 10–12.
specialist: If at school age reading is much harder for your child than for their peers, they often mix up letters, or they’re not progressing despite effort — talk to their teacher and a specialist (speech and language therapist, psychologist).

articles.title: Praise or encouragement?
articles.summary: Not “you’re so clever”, but “you worked really hard and tried another way”. Words that notice effort make a child more resilient in the face of challenges.
science: In psychologist Carol Dweck and colleagues’ famous experiments (1998), one group of children was praised with “you’re very smart”, the other with “you worked really hard”. Then, when a difficult task came along, the children called “smart” gave up sooner, exaggerated their scores and chose easy tasks. Those praised for effort took on the challenge more eagerly.

Another long-term study (Gunderson and colleagues, 2013) found that the “process praise” parents gave their 1–3-year-olds (“you’re working so hard”) predicted, five years later, the child’s belief that “abilities can be developed”.

This doesn’t mean giving up praise. Sincere, specific words focused on effort, strategy and kindness are the most helpful. Exaggerated praise (“you’re the best artist in the world!”), on the other hand, can backfire — especially in children with low self-confidence.
tryToday: Notice the process, not the result: “You rebuilt that tower so many times and didn’t give up!”
Be specific: instead of “Well done”, try “what an interesting way you mixed the colours”.
Ask a question: “What do you think of this drawing? Which part do you like best?”
Notice kindness: “You gave your sister your turn. That was really generous.”
mistakes: Calling every little thing “amazing”. Praise loses its value, and your child senses it isn’t sincere.
Praising your child with fixed labels like “smart” or “talented”. When things get hard, they avoid taking risks in order to protect the label.
Praising by comparison: “You read better than your brother.”

byAge.1-3: A simple description is enough: “You got dressed by yourself!” Share the joy together.
byAge.3-6: Name the strategy: “You put the big pieces in first — that was a clever plan.”
byAge.6-12: Appreciate mistakes too: “You got this problem wrong, but you found the mistake yourself. That’s real learning.”

specialist: If your child constantly says “I can’t do anything” or “I’m bad”, or falls into deep despair at small setbacks — talk to a child psychologist.

articles.title: Self-confidence: the “I can do it” feeling
articles.summary: Self-confidence grows not from praise, but from real skills, small risks and the belief that “you can do it”.
science: Children learn about themselves mostly from what they do and what they can do. Every time they do something themselves — put on their socks, sort out a conflict with a friend — the belief “I can do it” gets stronger.

When a parent solves every difficulty for their child, however good the intention, it can send the message “you can’t do this”. At the same time, a parent’s warm support gives a child the courage to take risks.
tryToday: Today, let your child do one task you usually do for them, even if the result isn’t perfect.
Instead of helping, ask: “What do you think we could do?”
Teach them the word “yet”: “I can’t do this yet.”
Help your child see their strengths: “You notice really quickly when someone is sad.”
mistakes: Protecting your child from every failure.
Comparing them with other children.
Shrinking their fear: “What’s there to be scared of?” Instead: “You’re scared, but I’m right here.”

byAge.1-3: Small independent tasks: taking their own shoes off, putting a toy back in its place.
byAge.3-6: Safe “small risks”: climbing somewhere not too high, saying hello in the shop themselves.
byAge.6-12: Support them in solving their own problem: let them talk to the teacher themselves, and practise together beforehand.

specialist: If your child avoids anything new, freezes in social situations, or fear limits their daily life — see a child psychologist.

articles.title: Chores and responsibility: by age
articles.summary: Chores aren’t a punishment — they’re a “contribution to the family”. Sharing jobs from an early age strengthens executive functions and self-confidence.
science: A study in Australia (Tepper and colleagues, 2022) found that children who regularly take part in household chores have better planning, working memory and self-control.

A two-year-old’s wish to help is natural. Brushing it off with “you’re getting in the way” leads to reluctance later. Small, real tasks give a child the feeling that “I have a place in this family too”.
tryToday: Give your child one age-appropriate “regular job”, and choose it together.
Break the job into small steps and show them with a picture card.
Don’t expect perfection. A badly folded towel is still a contribution.
Respond not with money or rewards, but with “thank you, that really helped us”.
mistakes: Doing every job for your child because “it’s quicker that way”.
Giving chores as a punishment.
Redoing what your child has done right in front of them.

byAge.1-3: Putting toys in the box, dropping dirty clothes in the basket, putting out napkins.
byAge.3-6: Setting the table, watering plants, pairing socks, feeding a pet.
byAge.6-12: Packing their own bag, helping make simple meals, taking out the rubbish, tidying their own room.

specialist: If your child has serious difficulty carrying out even the simplest sequence of tasks for their age, or is very easily distracted — talk to a doctor or psychologist about attention and executive functions.

articles.title: Stickers and rewards: when do they help?
articles.summary: A reward can help for a short while to get a new habit started, but it shouldn’t replace a child’s own inner interest.
science: A meta-analysis of 128 experiments (Deci, Koestner, Ryan, 1999) showed that an expected tangible reward for an activity that’s already enjoyable reduces a child’s intrinsic interest in it. The child starts thinking “I’m doing this for the reward”.

At the same time, in behaviour programmes, short-term sticker charts can be useful for getting difficult habits started (for example, toileting, morning routines) — especially when the reward is small, immediate and social (playing together).
tryToday: Choose one specific habit and set up a sticker chart for 2–3 weeks.
Make the reward time together rather than things: “5 stickers — we go to the park together.”
Once the habit has settled in, phase out the chart gradually.
Strengthen inner interest with words: “How do you feel when you get dressed by yourself in the morning?”
mistakes: Giving rewards for everything: “Read a book and you’ll get chocolate.”
Taking stickers back for bad behaviour.
Using food as a reward.
specialist: If no motivation system works and behaviour problems continue — look into parenting programmes and talk to a child psychologist.

articles.title: It’s OK to make mistakes: a growth mindset
articles.summary: How your child feels about mistakes is shaped mostly by how you feel about mistakes.
science: A growth mindset — believing that ability grows with effort — makes a child more likely to keep going, especially in moments of difficulty and failure. A large part of this belief comes from how mistakes are treated in the family.
When a parent treats failure as a “disaster”, the child avoids taking risks. When a mistake is treated as a chance to learn, the child is ready to try again.
tryToday: At dinner, everyone shares their “best mistake” of the day and what they learned from it. You go first.
When your child says “I can’t do it”, add: “…yet.”
Correct your own mistakes out loud: “Hmm, I forgot. Let me find another way.”
mistakes: Laughing at, mocking or punishing mistakes.
Correcting every piece of your child’s work so it’s “mistake-free”.
specialist: If your child shows excessive anxiety about mistakes, perfectionism or self-punishment — see a child psychologist.

articles.title: Fears and anxiety: small steps, not avoidance
articles.summary: Taking your child’s fear seriously while not letting them avoid it is the most powerful approach to anxiety.
science: Childhood fears are normal and change with age: in babyhood, strangers and separation; in the preschool years, the dark, animals, monsters; at school age, failure, illness and social situations.

The parent of an anxious child naturally wants to protect them from fear: not going where they’re scared, speaking for them, sleeping beside them every night. Researchers call this “accommodation”. It brings relief in the short term, but keeps anxiety going in the long term.

The SPACE study at Yale University (2020) showed that a programme teaching parents to accept their child’s fear with supportive language while gradually reducing “accommodation” was as effective as cognitive behavioural therapy delivered to the child.
tryToday: A supportive sentence: “I understand you’re scared. And I know you can handle this.”
Approach the fear in small steps: first look at a dog in a picture, then from a distance, then up close.
Notice courage: “Even though you were scared, you said hello in the shop yourself!”
In calm moments, read books and play games about fears.
mistakes: Mocking the fear or forcing them with “be brave”.
Shielding your child completely from everything they’re afraid of.
Punishing anxiety or belittling them with “you’re acting like a baby”.

byAge.1-3: Separation anxiety is normal. Use short goodbye rituals.
byAge.3-6: For fear of the dark, a night light and a “monster check” game can help.
byAge.6-12: Build a fear “ladder” together with your child: from the easiest step to the hardest.

specialist: If the fear or anxiety lasts more than a few weeks and gets in the way of nursery, school, sleep or friendships.
Panic attacks, compulsions to perform repeated rituals, frequent physical complaints (tummy aches, headaches) — see a child psychologist.
Nightmares after a traumatic event, re-enacting the event in play, regression — specialist support is needed.

articles.title: Lying: why children do it and how to respond
articles.summary: The first lies are a sign of cognitive development. Punishment doesn’t reduce lying — it makes children better at it; making the truth safe to tell is what works.
science: To tell a lie, a child has to understand that someone else knows something different, and build another version while keeping the truth in mind. That’s why the first lies appear at around 2–4 years and are linked with cognitive development.

In an experiment by Talwar and colleagues (2015), children threatened with punishment told the truth less often. On the other hand, a positive appeal like “if you tell the truth, I’ll be happy” increased truth-telling. In harshly punitive environments, children become more skilful liars.
tryToday: Don’t ask a question you already know the answer to. Instead of “Did you spill the milk?”, try: “The milk got spilled. Come on, let’s wipe it up together.”
Show gratitude when they tell the truth: “Thank you for telling me the truth. That was brave.”
Deal with the consequences of the mistake calmly, and don’t double the punishment because they told the truth.
Pay attention to your own “white lies”: “Tell them on the phone that I’m not home.”
mistakes: Calling your child a “liar”. The label reinforces the behaviour.
Punishing harshly after they’ve told the truth.
Treating made-up stories (“I saw a dragon!”) as lies. That’s imagination.

byAge.3-6: Help them tell fantasy from reality: “That’s an interesting story. Now let’s talk about what really happened.”
byAge.6-12: Look into the reason behind the lie: fear? embarrassment? When the reason is dealt with, the lying decreases.

specialist: If lying is very frequent, impulsive and comes with other serious behaviour problems (stealing, cruelty, running away) — see a child psychologist.

articles.title: Biting, hitting, pushing
articles.summary: At a young age, physical aggression is part of normal development — but it needs a calm, clear limit.
science: Long-term Canadian studies (Tremblay and colleagues) showed that physical aggression peaks at ages 2–3 and then, in most children, declines as language and self-control develop. In other words, children don’t learn to hit — they learn not to hit.
Biting and hitting often come from not having the words, frustration, tiredness, teething or a need for attention. Punishing a child by hitting them teaches the lesson “the strong one hits”.
tryToday: Stop it straight away and calmly: “No biting. Biting hurts.” Gently move your child away.
Attend to the child who got hurt first: “Let’s go and check on Ali — does it hurt?” This doesn’t give the child who bit an “attention reward”.
Teach an alternative: “Angry? Stamp your feet, or say ‘stop!’”
Note the patterns: when, with whom, before what? A pattern often shows up (tiredness, crowds).
mistakes: Biting or hitting your child back “so they know how it feels”.
Giving a long lecture. For a young child, a few words and action are much clearer.
Calling your child “aggressive” or “bad”.

byAge.1-3: If biting is linked to teething, offer a safe toy to chew on.
byAge.3-6: In a calm moment, play “what could we do?” with a puppet: the puppet gets angry and your child shows it what to do.

specialist: If aggression increases after age 4–5, often seriously hurts others, or there is cruelty to animals.
If aggression comes with speech delay, difficulties with social interaction or sudden mood changes — see a doctor.

articles.title: Sibling rivalry
articles.summary: Conflict between siblings is normal. A parent’s job isn’t to be the judge, but to teach them how to resolve conflict.
science: Conflict between siblings is very frequent: studies of young children have recorded several arguments an hour. It’s the first training ground for social skills.

Laurie Kramer’s research shows that the quality of a sibling relationship depends not on the absence of conflict, but on the amount of positive interaction and on conflict-resolution skills. Parental comparison and the feeling of a “favourite child” weaken the relationship.
tryToday: Spend short “one-on-one time” with each child separately.
In a conflict, don’t ask “whose fault is it?” like a judge. Instead: “You both want this toy. What can we do?”
Notice the moments they play together: “What a lovely castle you’re building together!”
Let each child have their own “untouchable” things.
mistakes: Comparing: “Look at your sister, she’s so tidy.”
Always telling the older one “you’re bigger, let it go”.
Stepping into every argument straight away. If there’s no danger, give them a little time.

byAge.1-3: At this age “sharing” is still a hard concept. Teach turn-taking with a timer.
byAge.3-6: Teach the steps of resolving conflict: everyone says what they want, you come up with three ideas together, and choose one.
byAge.6-12: At a family meeting, agree on fairness rules together.

specialist: If one sibling constantly harms the other physically or emotionally, frightens them, or one of them clearly doesn’t feel safe at home — see a family psychologist.

articles.title: When a new baby arrives
articles.summary: An older child’s jealousy or “acting like a baby” is normal. They need a place, a role and one-on-one time.
science: A new baby’s arrival is a big change for an older child: the parents’ attention, the rhythm of the day, the home — everything changes. Regression (asking for nappies again, baby talk, night waking) is usually temporary and a sign they’re looking for security.
Involving the older child in the preparations, giving them a small role with the baby and protecting one-on-one time with them reduces jealousy.
tryToday: Introduce the baby to the older child as “your baby”: “Look how curiously they’re watching you!”
Set aside 10 minutes every day just for the older child, and name it: “Now it’s our time.”
Offer them a helper role, but don’t force it: fetching a nappy, singing a song.
Allow their feelings: “Sometimes the baby wears you out, doesn’t it? It’s OK to say that.”
mistakes: Expecting the older child to be “big” straight away.
Starting nursery, changing their room or ending nappies at the same time as the baby arrives.
Punishing expressions of jealousy.

byAge.1-3: Play “looking after a baby” with a doll. Regression is normal.
byAge.3-6: Read books about babies. Let them express their feelings through drawing.
byAge.6-12: Give them “big brother/sister” privileges: a later bedtime, a special activity.

specialist: If the older child repeatedly behaves dangerously towards the baby — don’t leave the baby alone with them, and talk to a specialist.
If regression or sadness lasts more than a few months.

articles.title: Bad words and “toilet humour”
articles.summary: When a child tries out swear words, what matters most isn’t the word itself — it’s your reaction.
science: When children discover the power of words — especially words that get a strong reaction from adults — they try them out again and again. A strong reaction (laughing, shock, shouting) makes the word even more appealing.
A calm, short, neutral reaction, together with offering alternative words for expressing the feeling, is the most effective.
tryToday: Stay calm and keep it short: “We don’t use that word in our home. If you’re angry, say ‘I’m really upset’.”
If they don’t know what the word means, explain simply.
Set a time and place for “toilet humour”: “Those jokes are for the bathroom.”
Pay attention to the adults’ language too.
mistakes: Laughing at swearing or reacting with horror.
Humiliating punishments like washing their mouth out with soap.
specialist: If your child uses sexual words or shows sexual behaviour that isn’t appropriate for their age — calmly ask where they learned it and talk to a doctor or child psychologist. If you suspect abuse, contact {emergency} or the relevant authorities.

articles.title: Parental stress: put your own oxygen mask on first
articles.summary: The most important tool for calming your child is your own calm nervous system. Self-care isn’t a luxury — it’s part of parenting.
science: Harvard’s Center on the Developing Child divides stress into three types: positive (brief, manageable), tolerable (hard, but buffered by supportive relationships) and toxic (prolonged, intense, without support). The main factor that makes the difference is having a calm adult next to the child who “buffers” the stress.

When a parent is tired, hungry, sleep-deprived and alone, their ability to self-regulate drops, and shouting and harsh reactions increase. This isn’t a weakness of character — it’s the brain’s response to overload. In the WHO’s “nurturing care” framework, a parent’s mental health is considered one of the key conditions for a child’s development.
tryToday: Choose a “pause button”: when you get upset, take 3 slow breaths, with the out-breath longer than the in-breath.
Give yourself 10 minutes a day of time that’s just yours: a cup of tea, a walk, music. Take turns with your partner or family.
Prepare a sentence in advance for when your temper rises: “I’m really upset right now. I’m going to take a minute to breathe, and then I’ll come back.”
Celebrate small wins: if today you got through one hard moment without raising your voice, that’s a big deal.
mistakes: Trying to carry the whole load alone and seeing asking for help as weakness.
Trying to be a perfect parent. Children grow up beautifully with “good enough” parents.
Always putting your own sleep, food and health last.

byAge.0-1: When your baby sleeps, rest if you can — not housework. Share the night shifts.
byAge.1-3: Plan ahead for the hardest hours (usually late afternoon and evening): a simple dinner, fresh air.
byAge.3-6: Show your child your own way of calming down: “I breathe to calm down too.”
byAge.6-12: Share your feelings in simple words. Your child sees that adults have hard feelings too — and manage them.

specialist: If you’ve had sadness, loss of interest, sleep problems, hopelessness or excessive anxiety for more than two weeks — see a doctor or psychologist. Depression and anxiety in parents are very common and can be treated.
If you have thoughts of harming yourself or your child — don’t wait, get help immediately: {emergency}.

articles.title: I shouted — now what? Repairing the relationship
articles.summary: Every parent makes mistakes. What matters most for a child isn’t the absence of conflict, but restoring the relationship afterwards.
science: Edward Tronick’s research on mother–infant interaction showed that even with the most sensitive parents, a large part of interaction consists of “mismatch” moments. What matters is the “repair” that follows. Through repair, a child learns that the relationship can survive hard moments.
Repair is also a model for your child: making a mistake, taking responsibility, apologising and moving on. It’s hard to teach this with words, but children learn it by seeing it.
tryToday: Once you’ve both calmed down, get down to your child’s level.
Apologise without excuses: “I shouted at you. That wasn’t OK. I’m sorry.”
Explain your feeling without “but you…”: “I was really tired and I got upset.”
Share your plan: “Next time I get upset, I’ll try to breathe and talk calmly.”
Finish the repair with a hug or a small activity together.
mistakes: Combining the apology with blame: “I’m sorry, but you made me do it.”
Acting as if nothing happened. Your child remembers, and the silence confuses them.
Dropping the limit out of guilt. The apology is for the shouting, not for the rule.

byAge.1-3: Short and simple: “I shouted. I’m sorry. I love you.” And a hug.
byAge.3-6: Draw a “making up” picture together, or act out what happened with a puppet.
byAge.6-12: Ask your child: “How did you feel in that moment? What would help me?”

specialist: If conflicts and shouting happen very often and the relationship stays tense despite repair — a parenting programme or a family psychologist can help.

articles.title: On the same page with dad: co-parenting
articles.summary: Parents don’t have to be exactly alike, but it matters to agree on the main rules and back each other up in front of the child.
science: A child can adapt to two different parenting styles. What harms them isn’t difference, but open, unresolved conflict between the parents and putting each other down in front of the child.

A father’s active involvement — play, care, everyday tasks — is linked in research with a child’s positive social and emotional development. It lightens the mother’s load and lowers stress for the whole family.
tryToday: This week, have a 15-minute “parents’ meeting”: agree on 3 main rules.
Discuss disagreements later, not in front of your child.
Back each other up in front of your child: “Dad said no ice cream today.”
Let each parent have their own “special thing” with the child: bath time with dad, books with mum.
mistakes: Seeing dad as a “helper” and correcting everything he does.
Threats like “Just wait till your dad gets home”.
Using your child as a messenger between parents.
specialist: If there is constant tense conflict, threats or violence between the parents — contact a family psychologist or the relevant support services. If there is danger, call {emergency}.
