articles.title: Homework: help, but don’t do it for them
articles.summary: A parent’s role in homework isn’t “teacher” but “coach”: you organise the place and time and show interest, but your child does the work.
science: A review of homework research (Cooper and colleagues, 2006) shows that in primary school the effect of homework on academic results is small, and it grows in the higher grades. At a young age, the main benefit is the habit and the sense of responsibility.
Parental involvement helps, but it depends on how: a positive approach that supports autonomy increases a child’s motivation, while a controlling, critical, “doing it for them” approach reduces it.
tryToday: Set a fixed time and a quiet place. After school, a snack and some movement first.
Help them get started: “What have you got today? Which one will you start with?”
When they ask for help, don’t give the answer — ask a question: “How could you solve this? Which example could you look at?”
Break long assignments into 15–20-minute chunks, with short breaks in between.
mistakes: Doing the homework for your child or correcting every mistake.
Turning homework into a daily battle.
Excessive praise or punishment for marks.
specialist: If despite effort your child falls well behind their peers, has particular difficulty with reading, writing or maths, or can’t concentrate — talk to the teacher and ask for a specialist assessment.

articles.title: Friendship skills
articles.summary: Friendship is a skill that can be learned: joining a game, waiting your turn, falling out and making up.
science: Close friendships act as a buffer against stress for children and also have a positive effect on the quality of sibling relationships.
Some children pick up social skills naturally, while others — especially shy or impulsive children — benefit from practice.
tryToday: Invite a friend over and plan a short, structured playtime.
Practise joining a game: first watch, then offer something that fits the game: “Can I build a castle too?”
After a conflict, talk it through: “What did you want? What did they want? What could you do next time?”
Show interest in your child’s social life, but don’t interrogate.
mistakes: Solving your child’s friendship conflicts for them.
Insisting they “be friends with everyone”. One or two close friends are enough.
specialist: If your child shows no interest at all in friendships, has been completely alone for a long time, or is extremely anxious in social situations — see a child psychologist.

articles.title: Bullying: signs and steps
articles.summary: Bullying isn’t “just kids being kids”. Believe your child the moment they first tell you, and act together with the school.
science: According to UNESCO’s 2019 report, one in three students worldwide has been bullied at least once in the past month. Bullying is repeated, intentional aggression with an imbalance of power: physical, verbal, social (exclusion) or online.
Children who are bullied have a higher risk of depression, anxiety, sleep problems and avoiding school. Children often don’t tell because they’re ashamed or afraid things will get worse.
tryToday: Ask open questions about school: “Who do you sit with at break? Is anyone bothering you?”
When your child tells you, stay calm and show you believe them: “Thank you for telling me. This isn’t your fault.”
Arrange a meeting with the school — teacher, school psychologist, head teacher — and bring the facts (dates, what happened) in writing.
With online bullying, save screenshots, and teach your child how to block and report.
mistakes: Saying “just ignore it” or “hit them back”.
Confronting the bullying child’s parent on your own, emotionally.
A “punishment” like taking away their phone. It discourages them from telling you.
specialist: If your child is afraid of school, has unexplained physical complaints, belongings going missing, injuries, problems with sleep or appetite, or is withdrawing — talk to the school psychologist or a child psychologist.
If your child talks about harming themselves or about death — get help straight away, and if there is immediate danger call {emergency}.
If your child is bullying others — that’s also a signal that calls for specialist support.

articles.title: The after-school “meltdown”
articles.summary: If your child behaves well at school and then melts down at home, it’s a sign they feel safe with you.
science: At school and nursery, a child follows rules, holds their attention and manages their feelings all day. This drains their “reserve” of executive function. When they get home, next to the safest person, the built-up tension comes out.
Hunger, tiredness and sensory overload make this “meltdown” stronger. A short recovery time is the best prevention.
tryToday: When you pick them up: a snack, water, a hug — no questions.
Make the first 20–30 minutes at home “quiet time”: music, drawing, fresh air.
Plan homework and activities for after the recovery time.
Save the conversation for later: children often open up more just before bed.
mistakes: Greeting them at the door with “How did it go? What mark did you get? What’s your homework?”
Seeing the meltdown as “being spoiled”.
specialist: If the meltdowns are very intense every day, or your child persistently refuses to go to school — talk to the teacher and a child psychologist.

articles.title: Colic and a crying plan: for the hardest weeks
articles.summary: Some healthy babies cry for hours in the first months. A simple plan written in advance protects both your baby and you.
science: Doctors often describe colic with the “rule of threes”: a healthy baby cries for more than 3 hours a day, on more than 3 days a week, for at least 3 weeks. The crying often starts in the late afternoon or evening; the baby goes red, pulls their legs up to their tummy and nothing fully settles them.

The exact cause of colic is still unknown. The good news is that it passes: crying usually peaks at 6–8 weeks and eases a lot by 3–4 months. A randomised trial in Canada showed that mothers who learned in advance about this normal “period of crying” knew more about crying and were more likely, in a hard moment, to put the baby down somewhere safe and step away for a little while.

A lot of crying is one of the biggest sources of stress for parents. Tiredness wears patience thin. That is why half of the plan is for your baby and half is for you: who will help, when you will rest, and what you will do when your patience runs out.
tryToday: Write the plan on paper and stick it on the fridge: 1) check the basics (hunger, nappy, too hot or cold, wind); 2) two or three soothing techniques; 3) two people you will call for help; 4) a “when my patience runs out” step.

Try the soothing techniques one by one and give each a few minutes: holding your baby on their side in your arms, rhythmic rocking, a “shhh” sound, walking slowly, skin-to-skin contact, a dark and quiet room.
Keep a crying diary for a few days: when it started, how long it lasted, what helped. These notes are very useful when you see the doctor.
Set up shifts for the hardest hours: your partner, grandma or a sister takes the baby for an hour while you rest in another room.
When your patience runs out: put your baby down on their back in the cot, leave the room, breathe for 5–10 minutes, call someone, then go back. A crying baby is safe in the cot.
mistakes: Changing the milk, formula or your diet every day. Do this with your doctor, as part of a plan.
Giving tea, sugar water or “colic drops” without talking to a doctor. Some folk remedies can be dangerous for a baby.
Seeing the crying as your own failure. Colic is not the result of bad parenting.
Trying to carry everything alone. Asking for help is a strong step.
specialist: If your baby is under 3 months and has a fever, isn’t feeding, is very floppy or hard to wake, has an unusually high-pitched cry or is struggling to breathe: see a doctor straight away, and if it’s serious call {emergency}.
If there is frequent or projectile vomiting, blood in the stool, poor weight gain, diarrhoea or a rash: have your baby seen by a doctor.
If the crying doesn’t ease after 4 months or started suddenly: talk to your paediatrician.
If you have thoughts of shaking or harming your baby: put your baby somewhere safe and ask for help right away. It means your exhaustion has reached its limit, and help is available.

articles.title: Stranger anxiety and first separation anxiety
articles.summary: If your baby suddenly starts crying even in grandma’s arms, it isn’t a step backwards. They can now tell you apart from other people, and they are attached to you.
science: At around 6–9 months, a baby’s memory gets stronger and they begin to clearly tell familiar faces from unfamiliar ones. When someone they don’t know comes close, they may turn away, cry or cling to you. Psychologists call this stranger wariness and see it as a stage of normal development.

A little later, usually at 8–10 months, separation anxiety begins too: when you leave the room your baby cries, because they don’t yet know that you will definitely come back. This anxiety often peaks at 15–18 months and gradually eases.
What helps a baby calm down most is predictable, repeated experience: you go and you come back. The more often they live through this, the stronger their trust becomes.
tryToday: Play peekaboo: cover and uncover your face, then hide behind a piece of furniture for a moment. Through play your baby learns that “what goes away comes back”.
When guests come, don’t hand your baby straight to them. Let your baby stay in your arms first; you talk to the guest while your baby watches. When they are ready, they will show interest themselves.
Give grandma or a nanny the chance to spend time with your baby while you are there first. Then start with short separations.
Talk when you leave the room: “I’m going to the kitchen, I’ll be right back.” Hearing your voice comforts your baby.
When you part, keep the goodbye short and the same each time: a kiss, “I’ll be back”, and go. Don’t sneak out.
mistakes: Pushing a crying baby into a stranger’s arms “so they get used to it”. This increases the fear.
Shaming your baby as “spoilt” or “never leaves their mum”. This is a sign of healthy attachment.
Sneaking away. It seems easier in the short term, but your baby clings even more, because they are afraid to let you out of sight.

byAge.0-1: Peekaboo, “where am I? here I am!” games and short separations while they can hear your voice are the best practice.
byAge.1-3: Link the separation to a familiar event: “I’ll come after your nap.” A comfort object from home (a soft toy, your scarf) helps.

specialist: If at 9 months your baby doesn’t tell anyone apart, treats you and a stranger the same way, or avoids eye contact: see a doctor for a developmental check.
If separation anxiety is so strong that it disrupts sleep and feeding for weeks, or still makes daily life hard after the age of 3: talk to a child psychologist.

articles.title: Sleep regressions: 4 months and 8–10 months
articles.summary: If a baby who slept well suddenly starts waking often, the reason is usually rapid development. This phase is temporary.
science: At around 3–4 months, a baby’s sleep changes: the simple sleep of a newborn divides into stages similar to adult sleep. At the end of each sleep cycle the baby wakes slightly. If they only fall asleep in arms or while feeding, at night they look for the same help at every waking.
At around 8–10 months, other big changes pile up: crawling, pulling to stand, separation anxiety, teething. Your baby “practises” their new skill at night too, and looks for you.

Systematic reviews show that night waking in the first year is very common and the range of normal is wide. Many babies still wake once or twice a night even at the end of the first year. The word “regression” may sound scary, but it usually means a transition phase of 2–6 weeks.
tryToday: Look at daytime naps: an overtired baby wakes more at night. Keep awake times suitable for their age.
Keep the evening routine short and the same: bath, feed, lullaby. During this phase the routine gives stability.
Let your baby practise the new skill (sitting, standing up) a lot during the day, so they “practise” a little less at night.
When they wake at night, wait and listen for a few seconds: sometimes a baby makes noises between sleep cycles and falls back asleep on their own.
Sometimes try putting your baby down drowsy but awake. If it doesn’t work, don’t worry; you can try again later.
mistakes: Starting a completely new, strict sleep regime during this phase. First wait for the transition to pass, and choose the approach that suits your family. No method is compulsory.
Falling asleep together with your baby on a sofa or armchair while getting them to sleep. This is dangerous. If you are tired, put your baby in their own bed.
Cutting daytime naps “so they sleep well at night”. It usually has the opposite effect.

byAge.0-1: Around 4 months sleep cycles change; at 8–10 months movement and separation anxiety are added. Both phases often pass within a few weeks.

specialist: If your baby snores in their sleep, has pauses in breathing, sweats a lot or struggles to breathe: see a doctor.
If the waking comes with fever, ear pulling, vomiting or poor weight gain: it may be an illness, so have your baby seen by a doctor. For breathing difficulty or anything serious, call {emergency}.
If lack of sleep is wearing you down to a dangerous degree, or bringing sadness and hopelessness: talk to your doctor; help is available.

articles.title: Dummies and thumb sucking
articles.summary: Sucking is a baby’s natural way to calm down. The main question isn’t “is it allowed?” but “when and how to say a gentle goodbye?”
science: The sucking reflex begins in the womb and calms a baby. The American Academy of Pediatrics links using a dummy (pacifier) during sleep to a lower risk of sudden infant death syndrome. Breastfeeding mothers are advised to offer a dummy once breastfeeding is well established (usually after 3–4 weeks).

Long and frequent dummy use is linked to a slightly higher risk of ear infections. If dummy or thumb sucking continues intensively after the age of 3–4, it can affect how the teeth line up. Most children, though, drop the habit on their own between the ages of 2 and 4.
tryToday: Just keep the dummy clean. Don’t “clean” it with your own mouth, and never dip it in sugar or honey.
Don’t tie the dummy around your baby’s neck. You can use a short clip-on holder, but a long cord is dangerous.
If your baby loses the dummy during sleep, you don’t have to put it back in their mouth.
After the age of 1, gradually limit the dummy to sleep time only. During the day, other ways to calm down: a cuddle, a soft toy, a song.
Plan the goodbye together with an older child: a “dummy fairy”, “giving” the dummies to babies, or choosing a day on the calendar.
mistakes: Shaming thumb sucking, putting something bitter on their hand or punishing it. This can strengthen the anxiety and the habit.
Suddenly taking the dummy away during a big period of stress (a new baby, moving house, starting nursery).
Giving the dummy straight away at every cry. Sometimes your baby wants food, rest or contact.

byAge.0-1: A dummy during sleep can be helpful. Offer it once breastfeeding is established.
byAge.1-3: Gradually keep the dummy for sleep only. No dummy in the mouth while talking.
byAge.3-6: Involve your child in giving up the habit: a calendar, a sticker chart, an “I’m growing up now” story.

specialist: If thumb or dummy sucking still continues intensively after the age of 4, or you notice changes in how the teeth line up: see a children’s dentist.
If there is frequent ear pain or ear infections: talk to your doctor about the dummy.
If an older child sucks much more in anxious moments and there are other signs of anxiety too: consult a child psychologist.

articles.title: First foods: behaviour and appetite at the table
articles.summary: Moving to solid food isn’t only about what your baby eats, but how. A pressure-free, interesting and safe table is the start of a lifelong habit.
science: The WHO recommends introducing solid foods from around 6 months, alongside breast milk or formula. Signs of readiness: the baby sits upright with support, holds their head well, shows interest in food and doesn’t push the spoon back out with their tongue. Talk to your paediatrician about which foods to give, how much and in what order; the Anacan feeding section also covers this in detail.

This article is about the “how”. Babies often meet a new taste with a grimace the first time. That doesn’t mean “they don’t like it”. Research shows that offering the same food 8–10 times without pressure greatly increases acceptance.

Babies send fullness signals from the start: they turn their head, close their mouth, push the spoon away. Respecting these signals helps a child hear their own hunger and fullness later in life. In one study, when parents learned how to prepare food properly, there was no difference in choking between babies who fed themselves with their hands and those fed with a spoon. Whichever way you choose, what matters is the right shape of food and you being right there.
tryToday: Sit your baby at the table upright and supported, and give the meal with the family, without screens. Eat too, and let them watch you.
Offer the food, then follow your baby’s signal: if they open their mouth, carry on; if they turn their head, stop.
Allow mess. Touching, squashing and smelling food are part of learning. Put a washable mat underneath.
Offer a refused food again a few days later, without comment. Put a new food next to a food they like.
Prepare finger foods soft and long so your baby can hold them. Sit with them at every meal.
mistakes: Forcing the spoon into their mouth, saying “one more spoon for mummy”, or distracting them to get food in.
“Tricking” your baby into eating with a screen or toys. They don’t learn to feel how much they have eaten.
Giving hard, round and small foods (whole nuts, whole grapes, pieces of raw carrot). These are a choking risk.
Turning food into a reward or a comfort.

byAge.0-1: At first a few spoonfuls or small pieces are enough. At this age milk is still the main food.
byAge.1-3: Your child is learning to eat with a spoon by themselves. Give small portions and add more if they want. A picky phase may start; this is normal.

specialist: Gagging (the baby going red, pushing food forward with the tongue and making noises) is a normal protective reflex. Choking, however, is silent: the baby can’t cough, cry or breathe, and changes colour. In that case give first aid straight away and call {emergency}. Consider signing up for a first aid course.
Swelling of the lips or face, a rash all over the body, vomiting or breathing difficulty after a new food: this may be an allergy; if it’s serious, call {emergency}.
If at 9–10 months your baby accepts no solid food at all, gags or vomits with every bite, or isn’t gaining weight: see a doctor and a feeding specialist.

articles.title: The “fourth trimester”: the mother after birth
articles.summary: The first months after birth are a big transition not only for your baby but for you too. Asking for help and paying attention to your own mood are part of parenting.
science: The first 12 weeks after birth are sometimes called the “fourth trimester”. The body heals, hormones change sharply, sleep is broken up and life is rebuilt. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (2018) recommends seeing postpartum care not as a single check-up but as support that continues through these weeks.

Most mothers experience tears, irritability and mood swings in the first two weeks. This is called the “baby blues” and usually passes on its own. But around 1 in 7 mothers experiences postnatal depression: sadness, loss of interest and hopelessness that last more than two weeks. Excessive anxiety is also very common. These are not weakness; they are treatable conditions.

In the WHO’s nurturing care framework, the mother’s mental health is considered one of the key conditions for a baby’s development. A mother who gets support and can rest is able to respond to her baby more sensitively.
tryToday: Write a help list: who can bring food, who can hold the baby for an hour, who can do the shopping. When people ask “what do you need?”, name one job from the list.
When your baby sleeps, sleep for one sleep cycle too. The housework can wait.
Share the night shift with your partner: for example, a few hours you, a few hours them. If you are breastfeeding, they can bring and take the baby and change the nappy.
Ask yourself one question every day: “How am I today, from 0 to 10?” If it is low for several days in a row, tell someone close and your doctor.
Go out for a short walk once a day; you need daylight and movement.
mistakes: Carrying the whole load alone because “everyone manages, so I should too”.
Trying to host guests, keep the house clean and please everyone. In the first weeks, you and your baby come first.
Hiding sadness and anxiety with the thought “I don’t deserve to be a mother”. Many people have these feelings, and help exists.
Going only to your baby’s check-ups and putting off your own.

byAge.0-1: Mood swings are normal in the first two weeks. If they continue after two weeks or get stronger, talk to a doctor.

specialist: If for more than two weeks there is sadness, emptiness, loss of interest, hopelessness, being unable to sleep even when you have the chance, not feeling a bond with your baby, or excessive anxiety: see your doctor, your obstetrician-gynaecologist or a psychologist. Postnatal depression and anxiety are treatable.
If you have thoughts of harming yourself or your baby, or the thought “they’d be better off without me”: don’t wait, ask for help right away, {emergency}. Make sure another adult is with you.
Strange and frightening thoughts, hearing voices, losing touch with reality, or a lot of energy with very little sleep: this is an emergency, call {emergency} immediately.
High fever, heavy bleeding, shortness of breath, a painful swelling in the leg, a severe headache: these are urgent medical signs after birth, call {emergency}.

articles.title: Body safety: “my body belongs to me”
articles.summary: Knowing the correct names for body parts, the difference between “good and bad secrets” and that they can tell you anything protects a child. This conversation is not meant to frighten, but to empower.
science: Most sexual abuse of children is committed by people the child knows and trusts. That is why “be afraid of strangers” on its own is not enough. A child needs to learn that their body belongs to them, that they can say “no” to a touch that makes them uncomfortable, and that they should always tell you about it.

A Cochrane review (2015) showed that age-appropriate body safety lessons increase children’s knowledge and protective skills and make them more likely to tell someone what has happened to them. These lessons do not increase anxiety in children.
A child who knows the correct names for body parts can describe what happened more clearly. A child who knows their parent talks calmly about this topic can come to them in a difficult moment too.
tryToday: At bath time, name body parts, including the private parts, calmly and with their correct names. No tone of shame.

Teach a simple rule: “The parts your underwear covers are yours. Nobody should look at them or touch them, and you don’t touch other people’s. Only for washing and at a doctor’s check-up, with mum or dad there, is it OK.”

Explain the difference between a “good secret” (a birthday surprise, kept for a few days) and a “bad secret” (one that worries you, where someone says “don’t tell anyone”): “You can always tell me a bad secret, and you will never be told off.”
Respect your child’s “no”: if they don’t want to kiss or hug a relative, don’t force them. A wave or saying “hello” is enough.
Make a list of “trusted adults” together: who they can tell when you are not there (dad, grandma, a teacher).
mistakes: Trying to “settle” the topic with one long, frightening talk. Short, calm, repeated conversations work better.
Using shaming words for the private parts, like “the rude bits”. Shame keeps a child silent.
Forcing a child into adults’ hugs and kisses with “that’s rude, don’t upset grandma”. It teaches “someone else’s wish matters more than my feelings”.
Reacting with shock, anger or disbelief when your child tells you something.

byAge.1-3: The names of body parts and the idea of “my body”. Say what you are doing when you change their nappy.
byAge.3-6: The “underwear rule”, good and bad secrets, and the three steps “say no, move away, tell”. Practise with books and dolls.
byAge.6-12: Talk about it together with online safety: nobody should ask for photos or say “it’s our secret”. Talk openly about changes in the body too.

specialist: If your child tells you something: stay calm, believe them, listen, and say “thank you for telling me, it’s not your fault”. Don’t interrogate them, don’t press for details, and don’t bring them face to face with the person suspected. Make sure your child is safe.
If your child is in danger or abuse is happening now: call {emergency} immediately. Then contact the police, child protection services and a doctor; a child psychologist can help too.

Sexual knowledge or behaviour not suited to their age, pain, redness or bleeding in the genital area, suddenly starting fears, bedwetting, avoiding a particular person or place: calmly see a doctor and a child psychologist.

articles.title: Online safety: ages 6–12
articles.summary: Online, it isn’t bans but rules you set together, and the trust that “whatever happens, come to me”, that protect a child best.
science: According to the EU Kids Online survey (2020) in 19 European countries, a significant share of children aged 9–16 had come across something online in the past year that bothered or upset them. Children most often tell their friends and parents, but some tell nobody. When a parent is calm and non-judgemental, it is easier for a child to come to them.

Research shows that technical restrictions alone don’t fully protect a child. The best results come from filters and age limits combined with open conversation, using things together and clear family rules. The American Academy of Pediatrics calls this a family media plan.
The most common risks at this age: content that isn’t suitable for their age, online bullying, chatting with strangers, sharing personal information and photos, and hidden payments in games.
tryToday: Write your family internet rules together with your child: which device, when, where (not in the bedroom), which apps.

Teach four golden rules: you don’t give your full name, address, school or photos to someone you don’t know; you never go to meet someone alone; you share passwords only with a parent; if you see something that bothers you, close the screen and come to me.
Watch the game your child plays or the channel they watch together for 15 minutes. Ask with curiosity, don’t judge.
Set age-appropriate restrictions on devices and a password for payments. Don’t do it secretly; say “this is to keep you safe”.
Promise: “Even if you see or do something wrong, if you tell me, I won’t take your phone away. We’ll sort it out together.”
mistakes: Taking the device away straight after an upsetting incident. Next time your child won’t tell you.
Relying only on a filter. No app replaces a conversation.
Allowing a social media account that doesn’t fit your child’s age because “everyone uses it”. Follow the platforms’ age limits.
Forgetting your own phone habits. Children learn rules from example more than from words.

byAge.6-12: At 6–8, the internet only in a shared room and with you nearby. At 9–12, independence grows gradually, but the rules and open conversation continue.

specialist: If your child has been asked for intimate photos, or someone is threatening them, blackmailing them or asking to meet: don’t delete the messages, save screenshots, block the account and contact the police. If your child is in danger, call {emergency}.
If after online bullying your child withdraws, avoids school, or their sleep and appetite are disrupted: talk to the school psychologist or a child psychologist.
If your child talks about harming themselves or about death: ask for help right away, and if there is danger call {emergency}.

articles.title: Talking with your child about death and loss
articles.summary: Children grieve too, but differently: one moment they cry, the next they play. Honest, simple words and being there for them protect them.
science: The American Academy of Pediatrics (2016) recommends talking with children about death openly and clearly. Phrases like “went to sleep” or “went on a long trip” can make a child afraid of sleep or of trips. Simple words like “died, their body doesn’t work any more, they don’t feel any pain” are less frightening.

How a child understands death changes with age. A 3–5-year-old doesn’t yet fully understand that death is permanent and may ask the same question again and again. From around 6–8, a child understands that death can’t be reversed and can happen to anyone, which can bring new fears.
Children grieve “in waves”: the sad moment is short, then they go back to playing. This doesn’t mean they are less sad; they are simply processing a big feeling bit by bit.
tryToday: Say it with simple, true words: “Grandad died. His heart stopped. He doesn’t feel any pain any more. We will miss him very much.”
You can share your family’s beliefs, but also say clearly what death itself is: “We believe that … . And his body doesn’t work any more; he won’t come back.”
Answer questions, and if you don’t know, say “I don’t know, but we can think about it together”. Answering the same question many times is normal.
Don’t hide your own grief: “I’m sad too, that’s why I’m crying. Crying helps.”
Find a way to remember: drawing a picture, a photo album, cooking their favourite dish together. If your child wants, they can join the farewell ceremony after being prepared for it.
mistakes: Hiding the death or saying “went far away”. Your child senses the tension and becomes more afraid.
Seeing your child’s play as “disrespect”. Play is a child’s way of grieving.
Saying “don’t cry, be strong”. Allow the feeling.
Stopping the daily routine completely. A familiar rhythm gives safety.

byAge.1-3: Few words, lots of closeness: cuddles, familiar rituals. Your child feels the loss through you and the changes at home.
byAge.3-6: Explain many times, calmly, that death is forever. To the question “Will I die too?”:“I expect to live a very long time and to be with you.”
byAge.6-12: Your child asks more questions and may want details. Answer honestly, consider involving them in the farewell ceremony with preparation, and don’t force them if they don’t want to.

specialist: If after a few months grief still seriously disrupts daily life (sleep, eating, school, friendships), your child has completely withdrawn, or after a traumatic loss (an accident, violence) there are nightmares, fear and playing out the event over and over: see a child psychologist.
If your child says they want to go to the person who died, says they want to die, or harms themselves: ask for help right away, and if there is danger call {emergency}.
If you yourself can’t find your way out of grief: parents need support too; talk to a psychologist.

articles.title: Grandparents and the wider family: different rules
articles.summary: Grandparents are a great treasure for a child. Different rules aren’t a problem, as long as you can agree on the essentials.
science: In Azerbaijan, many families live with or close to the grandparents. Systematic reviews show that grandparents’ care is linked to children’s emotional wellbeing and to lower stress for parents. It is good for a child to have more than one warm, reliable adult.

Children are able to adapt to different rules in different places: one way at nursery, another at home. The problem isn’t that the rules differ, but adults contradicting each other in front of the child and not agreeing on safety matters.

Grandparents’ experience is valuable, but some advice has changed over the years: babies sleeping on their back, not giving honey or salt, physical punishment not being recommended. It is easier to talk about this not as an accusation, but as “this is what doctors say now”.
tryToday: Split the rules into two groups: “non-negotiables” (safe sleep, car seat, medicines, no hitting) and “things that can be different at grandma’s” (going to bed a bit later, an extra sweet).
Talk to grandma at a calm moment, without the child. Start with gratitude: “Without your help it would be hard. Let’s decide one thing together.”
Back up changed advice with something written: what the doctor said, an official guide. Not “this is what I want”, but “this is what the doctor recommends”.
Explain to your child: “Some rules are different at grandma’s house. At our house, this is how it is.” It doesn’t confuse them.
Let your partner talk to their own parents. When everyone talks to their own family, there is less conflict.
mistakes: Criticising the grandparents in front of the child. The child is caught between two people they love.
Turning every small difference into a battle. Save your energy for safety matters.
Teaching your child secrets like “don’t tell grandma”. A culture of secrets in the family is dangerous for a child.
Accepting grandma’s help but never asking her opinion. Respect is needed on both sides.

byAge.0-1: Give rules like safe sleep, the car seat and no honey in the first year in writing. A short “baby notes” sheet for grandma is useful.
byAge.1-3: Agree together on staying calm during tantrums and not overriding a “no”.
byAge.3-6: When your child says “grandma lets me”, calmly: “That’s how it is at grandma’s, and this is how it is at ours.”
byAge.6-12: Talk with the grandparents in advance about screens, sweets and pocket money. Children learn the differences very quickly and use them.

specialist: If there is constant, tense conflict between family members in front of the child, or the child is caught between two sides: a family counsellor can help.
If there is physical punishment, threats or humiliating behaviour towards the child: don’t leave the child alone with that adult. If there is danger, call {emergency}.

articles.title: A bilingual home: Azerbaijani and Russian
articles.summary: Growing up with two languages doesn’t cause speech delay. A child needs rich, lively communication in both languages.
science: Research shows that bilingual children reach language milestones (first word, first two-word phrase) at about the same time as monolingual children. Their vocabulary in each separate language may look a little smaller, but when both languages are counted together, their total vocabulary is usually about the same as their peers’.

Mixing languages (Azerbaijani and Russian words in one sentence) is not a sign of confusion. It is a natural skill of bilingual people, and over time a child sorts out which language to speak with whom.
How well a child learns each language depends on how much, and how lively, the communication in that language is. Language heard from a screen teaches very little compared with live conversation.
tryToday: Choose a family plan: for example, each parent speaks their own mother tongue, or one language at home and the other at nursery or school. Being consistent matters more than the plan being perfect.
Read books, sing songs and tell stories in both languages. If grandparents know one language better, time with them in that language is a big contribution.
When your child speaks to you in the “other” language, don’t correct them; just answer naturally in your language: “Yes, an apple! A red apple.”
Count vocabulary across both languages together, not separately: “mama” and “su” may be in one language, “мяч” in the other. They are all words.
mistakes: Suddenly dropping one language out of fear of speech delay. This usually doesn’t speed up speech, and it can distance the child from part of the family.
Correcting or teasing your child for mixing languages.
Trying to teach the second language only through screens and cartoons.

byAge.0-1: Speak to your baby in whichever language feels most natural to you. Feelings and songs are more alive in your mother tongue.
byAge.1-3: It’s normal for your child to prefer one language. Keep play and book time in both languages.
byAge.3-6: Sometimes a child doesn’t want to speak one of the languages. Don’t pressure them; create chances for play and friendship in that language.
byAge.6-12: As the school language gets stronger, support the home language with reading and writing: letters, books, family stories.

specialist: Bilingual children have the same speech milestones: if there are no gestures at 12 months, no words at all across both languages at 16–18 months, or no two-word phrases at 2 years: see a doctor and a speech therapist. Don’t wait, thinking “they’re bilingual, they’ll talk late”.
If at any age your child loses words they used to say or loses interest in communicating: don’t wait, see a doctor.

articles.title: Divorce and separation: how to talk with your child
articles.summary: What harms a child most isn’t the separation itself, but ongoing open conflict between the parents. Calm, honest and consistent support changes a lot.
science: Meta-analyses combining dozens of studies (Amato, 2001) show that most children from divorced families adjust well within a year or two. The main factors that raise the risk: long-running conflict between the parents, the child being caught in the middle, financial hardship, and losing contact with one of the parents.

The American Academy of Pediatrics (2016) recommends giving children a simple, age-appropriate explanation, reassuring them that “it is not their fault”, and keeping as much stability as possible in daily life.

Young children often link the separation to their own behaviour. Older ones may feel they have to “protect” one of the parents or choose between them. In both cases the child needs the same message: “This is a grown-up decision. We both love you.”
tryToday: If possible, talk to your child together, both parents. Short and simple: “Mum and dad won’t live together any more. This is a grown-up decision, it isn’t your fault. We will both always love you.”
Name the concrete changes: where they will live, when they will see the other parent, what won’t change (nursery, friends, favourite toys).
Make room for your child’s feelings: sadness, anger, silence, even relief. Say “whatever you feel is normal”.
Protect the daily rhythm: sleep, meals, nursery or school. Stability gives a feeling of safety.
Try to agree on the main rules and bedtimes in both homes. Make a calendar for your child.
mistakes: Criticising or blaming the other parent in front of your child, or saying “your dad/mum is like that”.
Making your child a messenger, a spy or a confidant: “Tell your dad that…”, “What does your mum do there?”
Asking your child to choose who they want to live with. You can ask their opinion, but the decision belongs to the adults.
Hiding the separation or giving a made-up explanation like “dad is away on a work trip”. Children sense the tension.

byAge.1-3: Stability more than words: familiar rituals, and their favourite toy in both homes. Setbacks (sleep, toileting) may happen temporarily.
byAge.3-6: Repeat the message “it isn’t your fault” many times. Your child may think “if I’m good, they’ll get back together”.
byAge.6-12: Answer their questions honestly, but without grown-up details. Support their relationship with both parents.

specialist: If your child’s sadness, anger, sleep or appetite problems or serious decline at school last more than a few months, or they blame themselves: see a child psychologist.
If the conflict between the parents doesn’t end: a family mediator or family psychologist can help find an agreement in the child’s best interests.
If there is violence, threats or any risk to the child’s safety at home: call {emergency} immediately.

articles.title: Moving house and big changes
articles.summary: A new home, a new city, a new nursery: change can be both exciting and a loss for a child. Preparation and steady rituals soften the transition.
science: The Harvard Center on the Developing Child divides stress into three types and stresses that change experienced alongside a supportive adult remains “tolerable stress”. The child learns to adapt to the new situation.

Systematic reviews show that moving very often, especially when the family faces other difficulties too, is linked to children’s emotional and behavioural problems. A single move, though, with good preparation and steady relationships, is a temporary difficulty for most children.
For young children the hardest part is unpredictability; for older children it is losing their friends and familiar surroundings. Both need time, explanation and a list of “what doesn’t change”.
tryToday: Tell your child about the change in good time: a week or two ahead for young children, earlier for older ones. Pictures, a map and photos of the new home or school help.
Make a list of “what doesn’t change”: we are together, the bedtime routine, the favourite toy, the call to grandma.
Give your child choices: let them choose where things go in their new room and what to write on their box.
Have a goodbye ritual for the old place: visiting their favourite park and friends, taking photos, an address to keep in touch.
In the first weeks, keep the rhythm of sleep, meals and play as much the same as possible.
mistakes: Hiding everything until the last day. Your child senses the tension but doesn’t know why.
Making several big changes at once: a move, coming out of nappies, a new nursery, a new baby.
Shrinking the feeling of loss with “it’ll be better there, no need to be sad”.

byAge.1-3: Play “moving house” with a toy house. Favourite things go in the first box and get unpacked first. Setbacks may happen.
byAge.3-6: Read books about moving or make your own “moving book” with pictures.
byAge.6-12: Make a plan for keeping in touch with friends, and find social opportunities in the new place, like a club or sport.

specialist: If a few months after the move your child is still sad and withdrawn, their sleep and appetite are disrupted, or they persistently refuse to go to nursery or school: see a child psychologist.
If the change is linked to a traumatic event such as a loss, violence or a disaster: early specialist support is helpful.

articles.title: Bedwetting: when it’s normal and when to see a doctor
articles.summary: Staying dry at night comes with the body maturing, not with willpower. Punishment doesn’t help; patience, and a doctor’s support when needed, do.
science: Staying dry at night takes three things: a hormone that makes less urine at night, a bladder that is big enough, and the ability to wake up to the signal of a full bladder. These systems mature at a different pace in each child. Bedwetting often runs in families: if one of the parents wet the bed as a child, it is more likely in the child.

About 15% of 5-year-olds may still wet the bed, and every year some of them start staying dry on their own. International guidelines advise discussing bedwetting that continues after the age of 5 with a doctor. Effective treatments exist.
A child doesn’t do it on purpose and is often very embarrassed about it. Punishment and shaming don’t reduce bedwetting; instead they damage the child’s self-confidence.
tryToday: Tell your child: “It’s not your fault. Your body is still learning to stay dry at night. It happens to lots of children.”
Let them drink enough water during the day, and cut down on drinks in the last 1–2 hours of the evening. No caffeinated or fizzy drinks.
Make going to the toilet before bed part of the routine. Keep the way to the toilet lit at night.
Keep clean-ups calm and short: a waterproof mattress cover, spare pyjamas. An older child can help with changing, not as a punishment.
Look at daytime toilet habits too: constipation makes bedwetting worse.
mistakes: Punishing, shaming, or talking about it in front of siblings.
Seeing waking your child at night to take them to the toilet as the only solution. Sometimes it only breaks your sleep and doesn’t teach dryness.
Cutting daytime drinks a lot. This doesn’t help the bladder grow.
Not seeing a doctor for years about bedwetting that continues after 5, thinking “it will pass on its own”.

byAge.3-6: Up to the age of 5, bedwetting is often part of normal development. Night nappies or special pants can still be used.
byAge.6-12: When your child wants to sleep over at camp or at a friend’s, make a plan with the doctor. At this age there are treatment options (an alarm, medication).

specialist: Bedwetting that continues after the age of 5: talk to your paediatrician and discuss the causes and treatment options.

If your child starts wetting again after being dry for at least 6 months, wets during the day too, or has constipation, pain or burning when passing urine, a lot of thirst and frequent urination, or weight loss: see a doctor.
If bedwetting started after a stressful event, or your child is very ashamed and withdrawn: alongside the doctor, a child psychologist can help too.

articles.title: Stuttering: when to be concerned
articles.summary: Stuttering for a while at the age of 2–5 happens in many children, and in most it passes. Calm listening helps, and some signs call for a visit to a speech therapist.
science: Stuttering most often starts between the ages of 2 and 5, when language is developing fast. According to research, a significant share of children stutter for a while, and most of them, about three quarters, recover on their own within a few years. It is hard to say in advance exactly who will recover.

Stuttering isn’t caused by a parent’s “wrong upbringing” or by a child being nervous. It has strong genetic and neurological foundations. But stress, rushed speech and correcting the child can make it worse temporarily.
Getting help early matters: speech therapy is more effective in the preschool years.
tryToday: When your child is talking, look them in the eyes and wait patiently for them to finish. Don’t finish the word for them.
Slow down your own speech a little and pause. Don’t say “talk slowly”; you talk slowly.
Set aside a few minutes a day for a calm, unhurried “just the two of us” talking time.
Set up a rule of taking turns to speak in the family, so your child doesn’t rush to “grab a word in”.
If your child talks about their stuttering, accept it calmly: “Sometimes words get stuck. That happens, and I’m listening to you.”
mistakes: Saying “stop, take a breath, say it again”. Your child pays more attention to their speech and the tension grows.
Teasing them about stuttering or discussing it in front of others.
Making your child recite poems or sing songs for guests.
Putting off getting help with “we’ve been waiting two years, it will pass”.

byAge.1-3: Repeating words and syllables (“ca-ca-car”) is common at this age. Listen calmly and keep an eye on it.
byAge.3-6: If stuttering lasts more than 6 months, consult a speech therapist. Treatment is most effective at this age.
byAge.6-12: Your child may avoid speaking or fear being teased. Talk to the teacher at school so there is support for spoken answers.

specialist: If stuttering lasts more than 6 months, started after the age of 3.5, or there is long-lasting stuttering in the family: see a speech therapist.
If your child shows tension when speaking (facial muscles tighten, blinking, head movements), gets “stuck” on words, avoids speaking or gets upset: don’t wait, see a speech therapist.
If there are other speech or hearing problems alongside the stuttering: get an assessment with a doctor and a speech therapist together.

articles.title: Pocket money: first lessons with money
articles.summary: Money habits start to form by the age of 7. A small amount of pocket money is a safe practice ground for making mistakes and planning.
science: A report prepared in the UK (Whitebread and Bingham, 2013) showed that key money habits, such as waiting, planning and understanding that money runs out, start to form in childhood, by about the age of 7.

According to a model from the US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, financial capability is built in three steps: executive functions (patience, planning), money habits and values, and then knowledge. Pocket money lets a child practise all three steps in real life.

Making money the “wages” for household chores can weaken inner motivation: “I don’t help without being paid.” Many experts advise keeping everyday chores that contribute to the family unpaid, with a separate agreement for extra jobs.
tryToday: Choose a small, fixed, age-appropriate amount and a fixed day: for example, once a week. Set the amount according to your family budget.
Set up three boxes or envelopes: “spend”, “save”, “share”. Let your child do the dividing themselves each time.
Don’t step in when your child spends their money on something “silly”. When the money runs out, don’t give more; calmly ask: “What would you do next time?”
Make a saving plan together for something big they want: draw a picture and let them mark each week how much is left.
Turn comparing prices in the shop into a game: “Which of these two packs is better value?”
mistakes: Turning pocket money into a tool for punishment and reward: “You behaved badly, no money this week.”
Giving a “loan” or extra money every time it runs out. Your child doesn’t learn to plan.
Talking about money only with worry, or hiding the topic completely.

byAge.6-12: At 6–8, keep it simple: counting coins, small purchases, a money box. At 9–12: a weekly budget, saving for a big goal, a supervised introduction to a bank card.

specialist: If your child often takes money from home or from others, or makes hidden, large payments in online games: talk calmly, look into the reason, and consult a child psychologist when needed.

If there is strong anxiety about money, saving everything and being unable to spend anything, or constant fear about the family’s financial problems: talk openly with your child, and see a psychologist if needed.

articles.title: Getting ready for first grade: what matters more than letters?
articles.summary: School readiness isn’t only reading and counting. Being able to wait, listen to a task, manage feelings and feel safe in a new place matters more.
science: UNICEF (2012) describes school readiness as a three-sided idea: a ready child, a ready school and a ready family. On the child’s side, health, language, social and emotional skills and an interest in learning all matter together.
Research shows that self-regulation skills (keeping attention, waiting for a turn, remembering rules) often predict success in the early grades as much as early reading skills, and sometimes more.
The American Academy of Pediatrics (2019) sees age-appropriate play, reading together, enough sleep and steady family routines as the key foundations of school readiness.
tryToday: Read together every day, and after reading talk about the story: “What happened next? What would you have done?”
Practise self-care skills: putting on shoes, opening and closing their bag, washing hands after the toilet, saying their name.
Play turn-taking games and games with rules: “Red light, green light”, board games, “Simon says”. These practise self-regulation.
Walk the route to school and around the building together. If possible, meet the teacher.
Over the summer months, gradually adjust the sleep schedule to school hours.
mistakes: Filling the summer only with letter and number “drills”. Play, conversation and independence help more.
Using school as a threat: “At school the teacher will tell you off.”
Comparing with other children: “The neighbour’s daughter can already read.”

byAge.3-6: In the last year of nursery, focus on skills like drawing, using scissors and glue, and listening to and carrying out short tasks.
byAge.6-12: The first months of first grade are tiring. Rest time after school and an early bedtime are important.

specialist: If at 5–6 your child has a lot of difficulty speaking in simple sentences, understanding a two-step instruction, holding a pencil or playing with peers: consult a doctor, a speech therapist or a child psychologist.
A vision and hearing check should be done before school: not seeing the board or not hearing the teacher can look like a learning difficulty.
If a few weeks after starting school your child still goes every day with fear, tummy aches and tears: talk to the teacher and the school psychologist.

articles.title: ADHD and autism: when to ask for an assessment
articles.summary: Not every active child has ADHD, and not every quiet child has autism. But some signs deserve an early assessment, because early support changes a lot.
science: This article is not for making a diagnosis. Only a specialist (a paediatrician, child neurologist, child psychiatrist or psychologist) can make a diagnosis after a thorough assessment. The aim is for parents to know when they should ask a doctor for an assessment.

Autism spectrum disorder is characterised by differences in communication and social interaction, and by repetitive behaviours and interests. The American Academy of Pediatrics (2020) recommends that all children are screened for autism at 18 and 24 months. Support that starts early has a better effect on communication and everyday skills.

The main signs of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are inattention, excessive activity and impulsivity. All young children show these signs to some degree. To talk about ADHD, they have to be much stronger than in peers, last at least 6 months, appear in two or more settings (home, nursery, school) and make life harder. A diagnosis is usually made after the age of 4.
tryToday: Observe and write it down: when, where, how often? Bring concrete examples to the doctor (for example, “when I call their name, they don’t turn 8 times out of 10”).
Look at the CDC “Learn the Signs. Act Early.” milestone checklist, or the milestone check in Parenting.
Ask the nursery or school teacher how your child is in the group. Some signs show up in only one setting.
If you are worried, don’t wait and don’t let yourself be silenced with words like “he’s a boy, he’ll talk late”. Asking for an assessment is your right.
mistakes: Sticking a “label” on your child based on internet tests or other people’s opinions.
Waiting months or years, saying “it will pass”. An assessment does no harm, but a delay delays support.
Seeing an active or impulsive child as “badly brought up” and punishing them. This hides the problem and damages the child’s self-confidence.
Explaining everything only by screens or sweets and putting off an assessment.

byAge.0-1: Watch for: at 6 months not smiling and “chatting” with you, at 9 months not reacting to their name, at 12 months no gestures such as pointing or waving.
byAge.1-3: Watch for: not showing you interesting things, very little eye contact, no words at 16–18 months, lining toys up but showing no interest in playing together.
byAge.3-6: Watch for: great difficulty playing with peers, very strong reactions to change, very narrow and intense interests; or being unable to keep attention anywhere, at nursery or at home, and constant dangerous impulsive actions.
byAge.6-12: Watch for: never being able to finish homework despite effort, constantly losing things, interrupting, persistent difficulty making friends, not understanding social rules.

specialist: If at any age your child loses a skill they had before (words, smiling, play): don’t wait, see a doctor right away.

If there are no gestures at 12 months, no words at 16–18 months, no two-word phrases at 2 years, no reaction to their name, or little eye contact and shared attention: ask your paediatrician for a developmental assessment and a hearing check.

If inattention, hyperactivity or impulsivity lasts at least 6 months, shows both at home and at nursery or school, and gets in the way of friendships, learning or safety: talk to a paediatrician, child neurologist or child psychiatrist about an assessment.
If your child harms themselves or gets into dangerous situations because they can’t control themselves: ask for urgent help, and if there is danger call {emergency}.
