sos.title: Lying on the shop floor, screaming
sos.moment: They wanted sweets, you said “no”, and now the whole shop is watching you.

steps.title: Calm yourself first
steps.text: Take one deep breath. What matters is your child’s safety, not the looks from other people. Most parents have been through this.

steps.title: Stay close, name the feeling
steps.text: Kneel down to their eye level. Few words, a soft voice. If needed, calmly pick your child up and move to a quieter corner.

steps.title: Stick to your decision
steps.text: Don’t change your mind: giving in makes the next tantrum stronger. Once they’ve calmed down, hug them and make a plan for next time.

say: “You really wanted those sweets. It’s OK to be upset. I’m here.”
“We’re not buying sweets today. At home we’ll cut up an apple together.”
avoid: Hitting, threatening or saying “I’m leaving you here” — it creates fear and doesn’t fix the behaviour.
Buying what they want to make them stop.

byAge.1-3: Distraction works really well: “Look how big that watermelon is over there! Let’s put it in the trolley together.”
byAge.3-6: Next time, agree before you go into the shop: “Today we’re only buying what’s on the list. You’re my helper who holds the list.”

sos.title: Hit their brother (or sister)
sos.moment: In a split second, play turned into a fight and the little one is crying.

steps.title: Stop it straight away
steps.text: Step in between them calmly but firmly: “I won’t let you hit.” If needed, gently hold their hand.

steps.title: Check on the hurt child first
steps.text: Comfort the child who’s crying. This avoids sending the child who hit the message that “hitting gets attention”.

steps.title: Then talk with the one who hit
steps.text: Once they’ve calmed down, name the feeling and teach another way. If they can, let them make amends: fetch some ice, offer a toy.

say: “You got really angry because he knocked the tower down. It’s OK to be angry, it’s not OK to hit.”
“Next time, say ‘stop!’ or come to me.”
avoid: Hitting your child to show them “how much it hurts”.
Long lectures and labels like “you’re a bad brother”.

byAge.1-3: Keep words few: “Gentle hands.” Separate the children for a while.
byAge.3-6: In a calm moment, act out the same scene with puppets and find alternatives together.
byAge.6-12: Go over the conflict together: what happened, what did you feel, what could you have done? Let your child suggest the solution.

sos.redFlag: If hitting happens very often or causes serious injury, or the younger child is afraid of the older one — don’t leave the children alone together, and talk to a specialist.

sos.title: Won’t go to sleep
sos.moment: One more drink, one more trip to the toilet, one more question… and it’s already late.

steps.title: Point to the routine
steps.text: Point to the picture bedtime routine: “Which step are we on now?” No arguing — let the card do the talking.

steps.title: Build the “last” things into the routine
steps.text: Make a drink, the toilet and a last cuddle part of the routine. Then say “the routine’s finished”.

steps.title: Return them calmly and boringly
steps.text: If they get up, take them back to bed calmly, with few words. The same every time, calm every time.

say: “I love spending time with you. We’ll carry on tomorrow morning.”
“Now it’s time for your body to rest. I’m in the next room.”
avoid: Scaring them: “If you don’t sleep, the monster will come.”
A different rule every night, or using a screen to get them to sleep.

byAge.1-3: Keep the routine short and exactly the same. A favourite soft toy can help.
byAge.3-6: Offer two choices: “These pyjamas or those?” Choice meets their need for control.
byAge.6-12: Work out their sleep time together (9–12 hours) and take screens out of the bedroom.

sos.title: Won’t leave the playground
sos.moment: You said “we’re going”, and they’re at the top of the slide shouting “no!”

steps.title: Give a warning in advance
steps.text: Say it 5 minutes before: “Two more goes on the slide, then we’re going home.” Show it on your fingers.

steps.title: Turn the transition into a game
steps.text: “Let’s hop like bunnies to the car!” or “Say ‘thank you, see you tomorrow’ to the slide.”

steps.title: If needed, calmly carry them
steps.text: Name the feeling and stick to your decision. Even if they cry, calmly pick them up and go. It isn’t a punishment, it’s a limit.

say: “You were having so much fun, you don’t want to go. I understand.”
“The playground will still be here tomorrow. Now a warm bath is waiting for you at home.”
avoid: Scaring them with “I’m going, you stay here!”
Saying “last time” again and again, then giving more time anyway.

byAge.1-3: A timer or a song makes the transition easier: “When the song ends, we go.”
byAge.3-6: Give your child a role: “Today you’re carrying the keys.” Or let them choose what you’ll do when you get home.

sos.title: They said “I don’t love you!”
sos.moment: After you said no, your child looks you in the face and angrily says “I don’t love you”.

steps.title: Don’t take it personally
steps.text: These words don’t mean there’s no love — they express strong anger. Your child chose the most powerful words they know.

steps.title: See what’s behind the feeling
steps.text: Name the feeling in a calm voice. Respond to the anger, not to the words.

steps.title: Confirm your love, keep the limit
steps.text: Don’t change your decision. Once they’ve calmed down, find other words together for expressing the feeling.

say: “You’re really angry with me right now. And I love you, even when you’re angry.”
“Next time you can say ‘I’m really upset!’, and I’ll hear you.”
avoid: Saying “I don’t love you either” or “then go and find another mum”.
Sulking or withdrawing your love.

byAge.3-6: Teach strong but harmless words for anger: “I’m going to explode!”
byAge.6-12: Ask later: “What felt unfair to you in that moment?” Sometimes you can explain the rule, or change it together.

sos.title: Bit someone at nursery
sos.moment: The nursery called: it’s the second time this week your child has bitten someone.

steps.title: Look for the cause
steps.text: Ask the carer when it happens: crowds, fights over toys, just before nap time? Are they teething?

steps.title: A short, clear rule at home
steps.text: “Biting hurts. We don’t bite.” Show them what they can do when they feel like biting.

steps.title: Be on the same page as the carer
steps.text: The same words and the same reaction at nursery too. Consistency changes behaviour quickly.

say: “No biting. When you’re angry, say ‘no!’ or stamp your feet.”
“Are your teeth itchy? You can bite this teething ring.”
avoid: Biting your child back.
Calling your child “the biter”.
sos.redFlag: If biting continues after age 3 and comes with speech delay or difficulties with social interaction, see a doctor.

sos.title: Won’t get dressed in the morning
sos.moment: You’re running late, and they’re hiding on the sofa in their pyjamas.

steps.title: Offer two choices
steps.text: “Red T-shirt or blue?” Choice reduces the “no”.

steps.title: Turn it into a game
steps.text: “Let’s see if you can get your socks on before the timer goes off!” Or let them help “dress” a toy.

steps.title: Get ready the night before
steps.text: Choose tomorrow’s clothes together the evening before. Fewer decisions in the morning means fewer arguments.

say: “It’s time to get dressed. Will you do it yourself, or shall I help?”
avoid: Repeating the same words dozens of times every morning.
Threats: “You’ll go to nursery in your pyjamas!” (if you’re not really going to do it).

sos.title: Explodes when you take the tablet away
sos.moment: Time’s up, you took the tablet, and now there’s screaming and tears.

steps.title: Announce the end in advance
steps.text: Agree before screen time starts: “When the timer goes off, the tablet goes for a rest.” Give a reminder when there are 5 minutes left.

steps.title: Accept the feeling, don’t give the screen back
steps.text: Calmly name the feeling. Put the tablet away out of sight.

steps.title: Build a bridge to the next activity
steps.text: Plan something fun and active for after screen time: a ball game, helping in the kitchen, going outside.

say: “It’s hard to stop right at the most exciting part. I understand.”
“You can watch again tomorrow at the same time.”
avoid: “OK, 5 more minutes” to stop the screaming.
Banning screens for a whole week on the spot as a punishment.

byAge.3-6: Have a “goodbye song” for the end of screen time, and let your child turn the screen off themselves.
byAge.6-12: Write the screen rules together. Children push back less when they helped write the rule.

sos.title: Refuses to eat at the table
sos.moment: They looked at the meal you cooked and said “yuck!”

steps.title: Don’t force them
steps.text: Say calmly: “You don’t have to eat. But the next meal won’t be until dinner.”

steps.title: Have a safe food there
steps.text: Always have something they like on the table: bread, rice, fruit. Don’t cook a separate menu.

steps.title: Move on to family conversation
steps.text: Close the topic of food and talk about your day. The less pressure, the more curiosity.

say: “In our home we don’t call food ‘yuck’. You can say ‘I don’t like this yet’.”
avoid: “One more spoonful, then dessert.”
Not letting them leave the table until their plate is clean.
sos.redFlag: If your child is losing weight, eats very few foods, or chokes, vomits or feels pain while eating — see a doctor.

sos.title: Baby has been crying for hours
sos.moment: You’ve fed them, changed their nappy, rocked them, and they’re still crying. Your patience is running out.

steps.title: Check the basics again
steps.text: Hunger, nappy, too hot or too cold, wind, something tight in their clothes, fever.

steps.title: Soothing techniques
steps.text: Swaddling (hips free), rhythmic rocking, a “shhh” sound, walking around holding them, skin-to-skin contact, a quiet dark room.

steps.title: If your patience runs out — take a break
steps.text: Put your baby down on their back in the cot, leave the room, breathe for 5–10 minutes, call someone. Then come back.

say: “I’m here, little one. I’m with you.” (Your calm, low voice affects your baby — and you.)
avoid: Never shake a baby. Shaking can cause severe brain injury.
Don’t blame yourself: some babies simply cry a lot in the first months.
sos.redFlag: If there’s fever (especially in a baby under 3 months), vomiting, refusing feeds, unusual drowsiness or an unusual high-pitched cry — see a doctor straight away; if it’s serious, call {emergency}. If you find yourself thinking about harming your baby, ask for help immediately.

sos.title: Clinging to your leg at the nursery door
sos.moment: The same scene every morning: crying, not letting go, and you’re running late.

steps.title: A short goodbye ritual
steps.text: The same every day: a hug, a kiss, a “special handshake”, then go. Drawn-out goodbyes increase anxiety.

steps.title: Be specific about coming back
steps.text: “I’ll come after your nap and snack time.” Not a clock time, but an event your child understands.

steps.title: “Hand over” to the carer and go
steps.text: Hand your child to a carer they like. Often they calm down a few minutes after you leave.

say: “Saying goodbye is hard. I love you, and I’ll come after your nap.”
avoid: Sneaking away.
Turning back at the door again and again.
sos.redFlag: If the crying hasn’t eased after a few weeks, your child is very anxious at home too, or sleep and appetite are disrupted — talk to the carer and a child psychologist.

sos.title: Told an obvious lie
sos.moment: The chocolate wrapper is in their hand, and they say “I didn’t eat it”.

steps.title: Don’t set a trap
steps.text: Don’t ask “Did you eat it?” Calmly say what you know: “I can see the chocolate’s been eaten.”

steps.title: Make the truth safe
steps.text: “If you tell me the truth, I won’t be angry. We’ll sort it out together.”

steps.title: Solve the problem
steps.text: Let the consequence be about the problem, not the lie: “Chocolate is for after dinner. Tomorrow let’s find a new place for it together.”

say: “Thank you for telling the truth. That takes courage.”
avoid: The “liar” label.
Doubling the punishment after they tell the truth.

sos.title: Said a bad word in front of guests
sos.moment: Everyone went quiet, and your child is very pleased with the effect.

steps.title: Don’t react big
steps.text: Don’t laugh, don’t look shocked. Calm and short: “We don’t use that word.”

steps.title: Carry on the conversation
steps.text: Shift the attention elsewhere. Without an audience, the word stops being attractive.

steps.title: Talk later, one to one
steps.text: Explain what the word means and why it can hurt, and find alternative words for anger together.

say: “That word hurts people. If you’re angry, say ‘I’m really upset’.”
avoid: Shaming them in front of everyone.
Humiliating punishments like washing their mouth out with soap.

sos.title: Crying over homework: “I can’t do it!”
sos.moment: Tears over the maths book, and angry scribbles in the exercise book.

steps.title: Take a break
steps.text: 5 minutes: water, movement, breathing. The brain doesn’t learn under stress.

steps.title: Break the big task into small pieces
steps.text: “Let’s just look at the first problem.” Success with one step gives motivation.

steps.title: Find the way with questions
steps.text: Don’t give the answer: “What do we know here? Which example looks similar?”

say: “This is hard, and you’re still learning. Mistakes are part of learning.”
“You can’t do it yet — don’t forget the word ‘yet’.”
avoid: Saying “But this is so easy!”
Doing the homework for them.
sos.redFlag: If this struggle happens every day and your child is falling behind despite their effort — talk to the teacher and ask for an assessment for learning difficulties.

sos.title: “You love him more than me!”
sos.moment: You gave the little brother some attention, and the older one stormed off to their room in a huff.

steps.title: Don’t argue, listen
steps.text: Instead of “That’s not true!”: “Sounds like you’ve been feeling left out lately.”

steps.title: Name what’s unique about your love
steps.text: No comparisons: “I love you because you’re you. Nobody else in the world could be my eldest daughter.”

steps.title: Plan one-on-one time
steps.text: 15 minutes just with them, today or tomorrow. Actions convince more than words.

say: “I love each of you differently, but with the same big love.”
avoid: “You’re the big one, you should be ashamed!”
Trying to divide everything with mathematical equality. Children don’t need equal attention, but attention according to their needs.

sos.title: Woke up scared from a nightmare
sos.moment: 3 a.m., and they come running into your room screaming.

steps.title: Comfort them
steps.text: Hug them, talk in a calm voice, turn the light up a little.

steps.title: Confirm they’re safe
steps.text: “That was a dream. Now you’re awake, I’m here, you’re safe.”

steps.title: Talk in the morning
steps.text: Don’t make them tell you the nightmare in detail at night. In the morning, draw it together and invent a “happy ending”.

say: “You got scared. I’m with you. The dream is over.”
avoid: “It’s just a silly dream, go to sleep!”
Scary films or the news before bed.
sos.redFlag: If nightmares happen very often or started after a traumatic event — see a child psychologist.

sos.title: Won’t sit in the car seat
sos.moment: Back arched, screaming starts, and you’re in a hurry.

steps.title: Safety isn’t up for discussion
steps.text: Calm and short: “If you’re not in your car seat, the car doesn’t move.” It’s a rule, not a punishment.

steps.title: Give a sense of control
steps.text: A choice: “You do one buckle and I do the other?” Or let them choose the song for the journey.

steps.title: Be patient, then say thank you
steps.text: If needed, wait for them to calm down. When they sit: “Thank you — now we’re all safe.”

say: “Keeping you safe is my job. We don’t drive without a seatbelt.”
avoid: Driving without the car seat because “it’s just this once, it’s not far”.
Scaring or hitting.

sos.title: Throws food and toys
sos.moment: The spoon is on the floor again. And they’re looking at you and laughing.

steps.title: Remember it’s an experiment
steps.text: At this age, throwing is a way of learning about gravity — and about your reaction.

steps.title: Give throwing a “place”
steps.text: “We don’t throw food. You can throw the ball.” Redirect the need to throw somewhere safe.

steps.title: It means the meal is over
steps.text: If they’ve started throwing food, they’re often full. Calmly: “You’re throwing, so you must be full. The meal’s finished.”

say: “Food is for eating. Balls are for throwing.”
avoid: A big reaction (laughing or shouting) — it makes the game more interesting.

sos.title: Snatches toys from a friend
sos.moment: At a playdate, a fight broke out over a toy.

steps.title: Calmly give the toy back
steps.text: “Ayan was playing with that. Let’s give it back to him.”

steps.title: Teach turn-taking
steps.text: “Ask for a turn: ‘Can I play with it next?’” Set a timer.

steps.title: Help them wait
steps.text: While they wait, offer another toy, and share their joy when their turn comes.

say: “You really want it too. Your turn will come.”
avoid: Saying “if you don’t share, you’re a bad child”.
Expecting real sharing before age 3.

sos.title: “I’m stupid, I can’t do anything”
sos.moment: After a mistake, they’re putting themselves down.

steps.title: Don’t argue straight away
steps.text: Instead of “No, you’re clever!”, notice the feeling: “You’re really disappointed.”

steps.title: Separate out the generalisation
steps.text: “This task is hard” is different from “I’m stupid”. Name the specific difficulty.

steps.title: Remind them of past successes
steps.text: “Remember, you couldn’t ride a bike at first either?”

say: “You made a mistake — that doesn’t make you stupid. It means you’re learning.”
avoid: Shutting down the conversation with “Don’t talk like that!”
Putting yourself down out loud for your own mistakes — your child copies it.
sos.redFlag: If your child constantly sees themselves as worthless, sadness lasts for weeks, or they say “I want to die” — get professional help straight away, and if there is immediate danger call {emergency}.

sos.title: I shouted at my child
sos.moment: Your voice went up, you saw fear in your child’s eyes. Now you regret it.

steps.title: Calm yourself first
steps.text: Breathe for a few minutes, drink some water. Don’t rush into talking while you’re full of guilt.

steps.title: Apologise without excuses
steps.text: Get down to your child’s level and take responsibility for your own behaviour.

steps.title: Complete the repair
steps.text: Share your plan and give them a hug. The rule still stands, but the relationship has been repaired.

say: “I shouted at you. That wasn’t OK. I’m sorry. I love you so much.”
“Next time I get upset, I’ll try to breathe and talk calmly.”
avoid: “I’m sorry, but you made me do it.”
Beating yourself up for hours. Repair matters more than the mistake.
sos.redFlag: If you can’t control your temper almost every day, or you’re afraid you might hurt your child — ask for help. If there is danger, call {emergency}.

sos.title: Came home from school in tears
sos.moment: They say: “They make fun of me, nobody plays with me.”

steps.title: Believe and listen
steps.text: Don’t fire questions, don’t interrupt. “Thank you for telling me. This isn’t your fault.”

steps.title: Gather the facts
steps.text: When, who, where, what happened? Calmly write it down. If it’s online, save screenshots.

steps.title: Act together with the school
steps.text: Arrange a meeting with the teacher and school psychologist. Tell your child the plan so they have a sense of control.

say: “You’re not alone. We’ll sort this out together.”
avoid: “Hit them back” or “just ignore it”.
A scene with the other child’s parent on your own.
sos.redFlag: If your child is afraid to go to school, has injuries, or talks about harming themselves or about death — get help straight away, and if there is immediate danger call {emergency}.

sos.title: Hit me
sos.moment: In response to a “no”, a little hand landed on your face.

steps.title: Protect yourself, stay calm
steps.text: Gently hold their hand or take a step back: “I won’t let you hit me.”

steps.title: Name the feeling
steps.text: “You’re really angry because I said ‘no’.” Low voice, few words.

steps.title: Show an alternative
steps.text: Once they’ve calmed down: “When you’re angry, you can hit a cushion or say ‘I’m really upset!’”

say: “Hitting hurts. I love you, and I won’t let you hit.”
avoid: Hitting back: “See how much it hurts?”
Laughing — it keeps the game going.

sos.title: “I’ve told you a hundred times, and they don’t listen!”
sos.moment: You call from another room, no answer. Your voice gets louder and louder.

steps.title: Come closer
steps.text: Don’t talk from another room. Go over, touch their shoulder, make eye contact.

steps.title: Say it once, briefly
steps.text: “Dinner in 5 minutes. Start tidying up your toys.” No long lecture.

steps.title: Follow through
steps.text: Instead of repeating yourself, stay with them and help them get started. When there’s action behind your words, they start being heard.

say: “Listen to me… Thank you. Can you tell me back what we’re going to do now?”
avoid: Repeating the same words ten times, louder and louder.
Threats: “I’m telling you for the last time!”
sos.redFlag: If your child often doesn’t react to sounds or doesn’t respond to their name — see a doctor for a hearing check.

sos.title: Bites or pulls hair while breastfeeding
sos.moment: You flinched with pain, and your baby is looking at you curiously.

steps.title: A calm reaction
steps.text: Gently take your baby off the breast (slip your finger into the corner of their mouth) and calmly say “ouch, that hurts”.

steps.title: Look for the cause
steps.text: Teething? Full and playing? Distracted? Feed in a quiet room.

steps.title: Offer an alternative
steps.text: A teething ring, and instead of your hair, a soft toy or a nursing necklace to hold.

say: “Ouch, that hurts. Here, have your teething ring to bite.”
avoid: Shouting or pushing your baby away — it can frighten them.
Thinking your baby is doing it “on purpose”. At this age they’re simply exploring.
sos.redFlag: If there are wounds, cracks or bleeding on the nipple, if every feed hurts, or if there is redness, a painful hard lump in the breast and a fever: see a doctor or a lactation consultant. A good latch and position often solve the problem, and you may not need to stop breastfeeding.

sos.title: My baby suddenly cries differently from usual
sos.moment: This cry isn’t familiar: higher-pitched, longer, and nothing helps. You feel uneasy inside.

steps.title: First look for signs of illness
steps.text: Take their temperature. Are they feeding, are their nappies wet? Are they floppy or hard to wake? Is there vomiting, a rash or difficulty breathing? Is a hair or thread wrapped around a finger or toe?

steps.title: If there is a danger sign, don’t wait
steps.text: Fever in a baby under 3 months, refusing feeds, an unusually high-pitched cry, floppiness, difficulty breathing, a bulging soft spot on top of the head: see a doctor straight away, and if it’s serious call {emergency}.

steps.title: If there are no signs, soothe and watch
steps.text: Hold them, rock them, a “shhh” sound, a quiet room. Note when the crying started and what you did. If you feel uneasy, calling the doctor is always the right step.

say: “I’m here. We’ll find out what’s wrong.” (A calm voice calms both your baby and you.)
avoid: Giving medicines, tea or folk remedies without talking to a doctor.
Saying “maybe it’ll pass” and not checking for danger signs. Your feeling that “something isn’t right” matters.
Shaking your baby. Never.
sos.redFlag: Fever in a baby under 3 months, refusing feeds, an unusually high-pitched or weak cry, floppiness, being hard to wake, difficulty breathing, a change in skin colour, vomiting, or crying after a fall: see a doctor straight away, and if it’s serious call {emergency}.

sos.title: My baby only sleeps in my arms
sos.moment: As soon as you put them in the cot, they open their eyes and cry. And you haven’t been able to move from the sofa for hours.

steps.title: Remember that this is normal
steps.text: In the first months, babies want to sleep close to your smell, your warmth and your heartbeat. It isn’t a bad habit; it’s a natural need.

steps.title: Soften the transfer
steps.text: Wait until they are in deep sleep (hands go loose, breathing slows), then put them down slowly. Keep your hand on their chest for a little while. Warm the bed with your hand beforehand, but don’t put pillows or a duvet in the bed.

steps.title: Protect yourself and your baby
steps.text: If you are tired, put your baby on their back in their own bed. Set up shifts: one sleep you, one sleep your partner or grandma. Some daytime naps can be in a baby carrier or on a walk.

say: “I’m not leaving you, I’m just putting you in your bed. I’m right here.”
avoid: Falling asleep on a sofa or in an armchair with your baby in your arms. This is one of the most dangerous places to sleep.
Putting your baby to sleep between pillows, on a soft surface or with a duvet next to them.
Leaving a very young baby to cry for a long time out of fear that “they’ll get used to being held”.

byAge.0-1: At 0–3 months sleeping in arms is very common. After 4 months, sometimes try putting your baby down drowsy but awake. If it doesn’t work, try again a few weeks later.

sos.redFlag: If your baby can only sleep upright, cries constantly when lying down, vomits, has difficulty breathing or snores: see a doctor. If you feel dangerously exhausted from lack of sleep, ask for help.

sos.title: I can’t take any more, I’m losing it
sos.moment: Your baby is crying, you haven’t slept, your hands are shaking. Anger and helplessness have filled you up.

steps.title: Put your child somewhere safe
steps.text: Put your baby on their back in the cot (a small child in a safe room or a playpen). A crying child can cry in a safe place. This isn’t abandoning them; it’s protecting them.

steps.title: Leave the room, 5 minutes
steps.text: Close the door, go into another room. Breathe out slowly, splash cold water on your face, drink some water, open the window. 5–10 minutes just for yourself.

steps.title: Call for help, then go back
steps.text: Call your partner, your mum, a friend: “I need help right now.” Go back to your child once you have calmed down. If you are not calm yet, wait until someone comes.

say: To yourself: “This will pass. I’m not a bad mother, I’m tired. I’m taking a break now.”
To someone close: “I’m very tired and I’m struggling to keep control. Can you come now?”
avoid: Never shake, throw or squeeze a baby. Even a few seconds of shaking can cause lifelong brain damage.
Trying to keep holding your baby while you are angry. Put them down first.
Hiding this feeling out of shame. Many parents go through it, and asking for help is a strong step.

byAge.0-1: This feeling comes most often at the peak of crying, at 2–4 months. Prepare a crying plan in advance.
byAge.1-3: In the middle of a tantrum you can leave your child in a safe place and take a short break. Say: “I’m on the other side of the door for a minute to calm down.”

sos.redFlag: If you are afraid you have harmed or will harm your child, if you have already harmed them (shaking, hitting), or if after being shaken your baby vomits, is floppy, breathes unusually or has a seizure: call {emergency} immediately. If this feeling keeps coming back, or comes with sadness and hopelessness: see a doctor or psychologist; this can be treated.

programmes.title: 21 days without shouting
programmes.summary: One small step each day: get to know your triggers, and learn to speak calmly and repair the relationship.
intro: Shouting is very often the sound of tiredness, rushing and an “I can’t take any more” feeling. This programme doesn’t expect perfection from you: just one small step each day.
If you shout one day, the programme isn’t ruined. Do the repair step and move on to the next day. Science says the same: what strengthens a relationship isn’t being flawless — it’s repairing.

days.title: Write down your why
days.task: Write one sentence about why you want to do this programme, and stick it on your phone screen or the fridge.
days.why: A clear goal sends the brain a “stop” signal in hard moments.

days.title: Find your triggers
days.task: Today, note every moment you want to raise your voice: time, place, what happened. Don’t try to change anything — just observe.
days.why: Recognising your triggers is the first step to managing them.

days.title: Your body’s signals
days.task: Notice what you feel in your body when your temper rises: a clenched jaw, a hot face, fast breathing? That’s your “amber light”.
days.why: Recognising anger early gives you time to stop before you explode.

days.title: The pause button
days.task: Choose a “stop” action: put your hand on your heart, or take a step back. Use it at least once today.
days.why: A physical action interrupts the automatic reaction and buys time for the thinking brain.

days.title: A long out-breath
days.task: When you get upset, take 3 breaths: breathe in for 4 seconds, breathe out for 6 seconds. Practise once in the morning too.
days.why: A long out-breath slows the heart rate and switches off the stress response.

days.title: Come close, then talk
days.task: Today, don’t call your child from another room. Each time, go over to them, make eye contact, then talk.
days.why: When you talk from a distance, your voice rises automatically; up close, your child hears you better.

days.title: Celebrate one week
days.task: Look back at the first week: which moment was hardest, what helped? Give yourself a small treat.
days.why: Noticing small wins keeps you motivated.

days.title: Hungry, tired hours
days.task: Make a plan for the hardest time of day: for example, in the late afternoon, you and your child both have a snack.
days.why: Hunger and tiredness reduce everyone’s ability to self-regulate.

days.title: Drop to a whisper
days.task: Today, when you get upset, lower your voice instead of raising it. Your child calms down to hear the whisper — and so do you.
days.why: An unexpectedly quiet voice catches attention and reduces tension.

days.title: A repair conversation
days.task: If you’ve shouted this week, have a short repair conversation with your child: apologise, share your plan, hug.
days.why: Repair shows your child that the relationship is safe and how to recover from a mistake.

days.title: One sentence, once
days.task: Say your request once, short and clear, then back it up with action (stay next to them, help them get started).
days.why: Repeated words lose their value; action convinces.

days.title: Where you can say “yes”
days.task: Today, instead of “no”, try the “yes, … later” formula: “Yes, you can watch a cartoon — after dinner.”
days.why: Positive framing reduces resistance and increases cooperation.

days.title: Set the scene in advance
days.task: Pick the moment with the most arguments (morning, bedtime) and prepare the evening before: clothes, bag, picture plan.
days.why: Preparation reduces rushing — and rushed moments are when shouting is most likely.

days.title: Two-week celebration
days.task: You’re halfway there! Tell your child too: “I’m learning to talk more calmly.” Ask what they think.
days.why: Involving your child in the process makes them a member of the calm-down team too.

days.title: Put your feelings into words
days.task: Instead of shouting, say how you feel: “I’m getting really upset right now. I need a minute to calm down.”
days.why: This shows your child how to put their own feelings into words too.

days.title: Ask for help
days.task: Agree on a “tag-out signal” with your partner or someone close: when one of you gets upset, the other takes over.
days.why: Nobody can stay calm all the time on their own; a team lightens the load.

days.title: Your own time
days.task: Today, set aside 15 minutes for yourself: a walk, a cup of tea, music. Write it into your plan.
days.why: A rested parent has more patience.

days.title: Catch the good
days.task: Today, notice and name 5 good behaviours from your child.
days.why: As positive attention increases, problem behaviour — and the shouting that comes with it — decreases.

days.title: Cooperation through play
days.task: Turn one task into a game: a race to tidy the toys, a song for brushing teeth.
days.why: Play reduces tension and increases your child’s willingness to cooperate.

days.title: Write your plan
days.task: Write your own “calm-down plan” for the future: 3 triggers, 3 strategies, 1 repair sentence.
days.why: A written plan keeps the habit alive after the programme ends.

days.title: Look back and celebrate
days.task: Look back over the 21 days: what has changed? Have a small celebration with your child, and thank yourself.
days.why: Noticing and celebrating change strengthens the new habit.

programmes.title: 14 days with tantrums
programmes.summary: A two-week path to understanding tantrums, preventing them and staying calm in the hardest moments.
intro: A tantrum is the moment when your child’s brain hasn’t yet learned to manage big feelings. Over these 14 days, the goal isn’t to make tantrums disappear completely, but to make them fewer and shorter, and to get through them together more calmly.

days.title: Tantrum diary
days.task: Today, note down every tantrum: time, cause, how long it lasted, what you did.
days.why: Patterns (tiredness, hunger, transitions) only show up when you observe.

days.title: Hunger and sleep
days.task: Check meal and sleep times. Today, move a snack to just before the tantrum hours.
days.why: A hungry, tired brain finds feelings harder to manage.

days.title: Transition warnings
days.task: Give a heads-up 5 minutes before every transition: “Two more times, then it’s bath time.”
days.why: Unexpected change is the most common cause of tantrums.

days.title: Choices
days.task: During the day, offer two choices at least 5 times: “This cup or that one?”
days.why: A sense of control reduces the need to say “no” and to have a tantrum.

days.title: Name the feeling
days.task: Today, in every hard moment, name the feeling: “You’re disappointed.” Don’t say more than that.
days.why: A named feeling calms the brain’s emotion centre.

days.title: A calm body
days.task: During a tantrum, pay attention to your own body: drop your shoulders, sit down, lower your voice.
days.why: Your child “borrows” calm from your calm body.

days.title: One-week review
days.task: Look at your diary: are tantrums fewer, shorter? What helped most?
days.why: Seeing small progress gives you the strength to keep going.

days.title: Practise when calm
days.task: At a calm time, play the “flower and candle” breathing game with your child.
days.why: Skills are learned in calm times and used in hard moments.

days.title: A feelings book
days.task: Read a book about feelings together, or draw faces: happy, angry, sad, scared.
days.why: Having words for feelings helps replace tantrums with words.

days.title: Cosy corner
days.task: Set up a cosy corner at home together: a cushion, a soft toy, a book.
days.why: A safe place to calm down strengthens self-regulation.

days.title: Stick to your decision
days.task: Today, with one thing you’ve said “no” to, kindly stick to your decision despite the tantrum.
days.why: Consistency teaches your child that a tantrum doesn’t change the decision, and over time it reduces tantrums.

days.title: Hug and repair
days.task: After every tantrum, give a hug and say a few words: “That was hard. You calmed down.”
days.why: Repair strengthens the relationship and shows your child their success.

days.title: Notice the good moments
days.task: Find a moment when your child was disappointed but stayed calm, and name it: “You really wanted it, but you waited!”
days.why: The behaviour we notice is the behaviour that grows.

days.title: Write your plan
days.task: Your “tantrum plan”: 3 prevention steps, 3 in-the-moment steps, 1 repair ritual.
days.why: A written plan keeps new habits going after the programme ends.

programmes.title: 7-day sleep routine
programmes.summary: Build a calm, predictable bedtime routine in one week. No crying it out, no rush.
intro: Research shows that a simple routine repeated every evening helps children fall asleep faster and wake less at night within just one or two weeks. This programme doesn’t require any “cry it out” method; you choose the approach that suits your family.
For babies under 6 months, night feeds and waking are normal; for them, this programme only helps build the routine.

days.title: Write down where you are now
days.task: This evening, note: what time they went to bed, how many minutes it took to fall asleep, how many times they woke in the night.
days.why: You need a starting point to see change.

days.title: A fixed bedtime
days.task: Work out the sleep your child needs for their age and choose a fixed bedtime. Today, move 15 minutes closer to it.
days.why: A fixed time regulates the body’s internal clock.

days.title: A screen-free hour
days.task: Turn off all screens and dim the lights 1 hour before sleep.
days.why: Screen light and exciting content delay falling asleep.

days.title: A three-step routine
days.task: Build the routine: for example, bath → pyjamas and teeth → book and lullaby. Do the whole thing for the first time this evening.
days.why: The same order every evening signals to the brain that “sleep is coming”.

days.title: Picture card
days.task: Show the routine steps on a card with pictures; let your child tick off each step themselves.
days.why: A visible plan reduces arguments and gives your child a sense of control.

days.title: A calm goodnight
days.task: At the end of the routine, say the same calm sentence: “Goodnight, see you in the morning.” Respond to night waking calmly and with few words too.
days.why: Predictable, boring night-time responses reduce waking.

days.title: Look at the results
days.task: Compare with your notes from the first day. Keep the routine going; change often shows within 1–2 weeks.
days.why: Consistency is the foundation of a sleep habit.

programmes.title: Sibling harmony in 7 days
programmes.summary: In one week, move from being the referee to being the coach: give each child their own place and teach them to solve conflicts together.
intro: Sibling arguments are normal and are the first practice ground for social skills. The aim of this programme isn’t to make arguments disappear completely, but to reduce them and teach children to resolve them themselves.
Research shows that a sibling relationship is strengthened not by the absence of conflict but by plenty of positive moments together. One small step a day is enough.

days.title: Observation day
days.task: Today, note the arguments: when, over what, who started it, what you did. Wait 10 seconds before stepping in.
days.why: Most arguments happen at the same times and for the same reasons. Once you see the pattern, it becomes easier to prevent them.

days.title: 10 minutes each
days.task: Spend 10 minutes alone with each child, and let them choose the game. Give it a name: “This is our time.”
days.why: A child whose need for attention is met has less need to win it by competing with their sibling.

days.title: A day without comparisons
days.task: Make no comparisons today: no “look at your sister”, no “be like your brother”. Compare each child only with themselves: “Yesterday you couldn’t, today you did it up yourself!”
days.why: Comparison strengthens rivalry and the feeling of a “favourite child”.

days.title: Off-limits things
days.task: Let each child choose three “only mine” things. Keep them in a separate box. For the rest of the toys, set up a turn-taking rule with a timer.
days.why: A child whose own boundary is protected is more ready to share.

days.title: Problem-solving steps
days.task: At the next argument, don’t be the referee. Three steps: everyone says what they want, you find three ideas together, you choose one.
days.why: As children resolve conflict themselves, they master this skill and rely less on the parent.

days.title: A team task
days.task: Give the children a job to do together: decorating a cake, building a fort, watering a plant. Notice and name their success together.
days.why: A shared goal and a shared success strengthen the sibling bond.

days.title: Family meeting
days.task: Hold a short family meeting: what went well this week, which rule worked? Let the children suggest one rule for next week.
days.why: A child who is the author of a rule follows it more, and the sense of fairness grows.

programmes.title: Screen time reset in 7 days
programmes.summary: Rebuild your family’s relationship with screens without bans and shouting: a family plan, screen-free zones and interesting things to do after the screen.
intro: The screen itself isn’t the enemy, but it becomes a problem when it crowds out sleep, movement and time together. This week the aim isn’t to suddenly ban screens completely, but to turn screen time into time managed by family rules.
The change applies to the whole family: adults’ phone habits are part of this programme too. There may be tantrums on some days; this is normal and usually eases within a few days.

days.title: Where things stand
days.task: Change nothing today, just note: how much your child and you look at screens, when, and at which moments the screen becomes a “soother”.
days.why: To see change you need a starting point, and the numbers often surprise us.

days.title: Screen-free zones
days.task: Set two screen-free zones: the dinner table and the bedroom. For everyone, adults included.
days.why: Screens at meals and before bed disrupt fullness signals and sleep.

days.title: Announce the end in advance
days.task: Before every screen session, agree: how long, and when it ends. Set a timer and give a reminder 5 minutes before.
days.why: A predictable end makes the transition easier and reduces tantrums.

days.title: A bridge after the screen
days.task: Plan something interesting for right after the screen ends: a ball game, helping in the kitchen, going outside, drawing together.
days.why: Leaving the screen is easier when there is an appealing alternative, not emptiness.

days.title: Watch together
days.task: Today, watch together with your child once and talk: “Why do you think they did that? What would you have done?”
days.why: Watching together turns the screen from passive time into time for connection.

days.title: Grown-ups’ phones
days.task: This evening, for 1 hour while you are with your child, put your phone in another room and turn off notifications.
days.why: Children learn rules from example more than from words. A parent distracted by their phone also means less connection.

days.title: Family media plan
days.task: Make a written family media plan together: where, when, how much, what content. Hang it somewhere visible.
days.why: A plan written together gives a child a sense of control and makes them more likely to follow the rules.

programmes.title: 10 minutes of special time a day: 7 days
programmes.summary: A 10-minute, child-led play session every day. A small habit with a big effect: less struggle, more closeness.
intro: Special time is a core part of some of the most researched parenting programmes (for example, PCIT): every day for a short time the child chooses the play, and the parent follows, describes and praises.
This time isn’t a reward or a punishment; it’s a daily “vitamin”. Don’t cancel it even on a bad day. Within a week you will see how this simple ritual works.

days.title: Choose a time and place
days.task: Find 10 minutes in the day that can happen at the same time every day. Tell your child: “Every day we’ll have special time together, and you’ll choose the game.” Do it for the first time today.
days.why: A predictable time shows your child that your attention will definitely come.

days.title: Phone in another room
days.task: Set a timer and put your phone in another room. Let your child choose the game, and you follow. No commands, questions or criticism.
days.why: Full attention is one of a child’s strongest needs, and divided attention doesn’t meet it.

days.title: Be a sports commentator
days.task: Today, describe what your child is doing: “You put the red car into the tunnel. Now you’re building the tower tall.”
days.why: Describing makes your child feel seen and at the same time enriches their language.

days.title: Copy them
days.task: Copy your child’s play: they place a block, and you place the same block next to it. Don’t try to change the game.
days.why: Copying sends the message “your ideas matter” and boosts your child’s self-confidence.

days.title: Specific praise
days.task: Today during special time, give specific praise three times: “You’re building so patiently!”, “You gave me a colour too, thank you!”
days.why: Specific praise shows which behaviour was noticed and strengthens it.

days.title: Keep going on a hard day
days.task: Don’t cancel special time today even if it’s a hard day. If your child breaks a rule during play, briefly turn your attention elsewhere, then carry on.
days.why: When special time is unconditional, it repairs the relationship and reduces behaviour problems in the long term.

days.title: What has changed?
days.task: Look back over the week: what has changed in your child’s behaviour and in your relationship? Ask your child: “What did you like most about our special time?” Plan to keep going.
days.why: Seeing the change keeps the habit alive after the programme too.

styleQuiz.title: My parenting style
styleQuiz.intro: 12 short statements. Think about the last two weeks and answer honestly — there are no right or wrong answers here. Your result is saved in your account and only you can see it.

items.text: When my child is sad or angry, I name the feeling and stay with them.
During the day I find time to hug them, laugh together and say “I love you”.
When my child talks to me, I put my phone aside and listen.
I notice their good behaviour and name it.
At home we have a few clear rules that my child knows.
Once I’ve set a rule, I calmly follow through on it.
Our daily routine (meals, sleep) is more or less consistent.
When my child cries or insists, I go back on the “no” I gave.
When I’m tired, I drop the rules completely — “let them do whatever they want”.
When I get upset, I raise my voice or shout.
I threaten my child (“I’ll leave you here”, “I’ll call the police”).
In moments of anger I feel the urge to hit them or say harsh words, and sometimes I do.

balanced.title: Warm and clear
balanced.short: You show love and also set clear limits — the combination research considers the most beneficial.
detail: Psychologists call this style “authoritative”: high warmth and high structure. On average, children raised with this style are more independent and self-confident and manage their feelings better.
This doesn’t mean being perfect. You get tired too, and sometimes your patience runs out. What makes the difference is coming back to the relationship after hard moments.
next: As your child grows, start making rules together with them.
Don’t forget to look after yourself: to be a calm parent, you need rest.
Protect your “special time” habit — it’s your strongest “insurance”.

gentle.title: Very warm, gentle limits
gentle.short: You’re very close to your child and sensitive to their feelings. Sometimes holding limits feels hard.
detail: Warmth is your greatest strength, and it’s invaluable for your child’s secure attachment. But children test limits to find out whether they’re still there. When limits soften, children test more — and parents get worn out.
Love and limits don’t contradict each other. Saying “I love you, and the answer is still no” gives your child a sense of safety.
next: Choose 3–5 clear family rules and apply them calmly.
Show empathy during tantrums, but don’t change your decision.
Try the “one sentence, once” step from the “21 days without shouting” programme.

storm.title: Loving, but explodes when tired
storm.short: You’re very attached to your child, but in stressful moments your voice goes up. Lots of parents recognise this.
detail: Your warmth is a strong foundation. Shouting and harsh words are very often the result of tiredness, rushing and being on your own — not a lack of love.

Research shows that regular shouting has a negative effect on children’s behaviour even when the relationship is warm. The good news: self-regulation is a skill that can be learned, and repair conversations protect the relationship.
next: Find your triggers: which times of day, which situations?
Start with the “pause button” and a long out-breath.
The “21 days without shouting” programme is made for you.

strict.title: Strong limits, hidden warmth
strict.short: You value order and rules. Sometimes that comes at the cost of warmth and listening.
detail: Rules and consistency matter for children — this is your strength. But according to research, limits set through harsh control and punishment don’t reduce behaviour problems in the long run — they can even increase them.
You can keep the rules and still add more warmth: explaining, naming feelings, noticing good behaviour.
next: 10 minutes a day of play led by your child.
Use logical consequences instead of punishment.
Explain one rule: “We have this rule because…”

stretched.title: Tired and drained
stretched.short: It looks like you’ve been very tired lately. That doesn’t make you a bad parent — it’s a signal that you need support.
detail: When a parent is drained, there’s no energy left for either warmth or structure. It’s a very common and understandable situation, especially with a baby, lack of sleep, work and being on your own.
This result isn’t an accusation — it shows that you need care too. Small steps and asking for help can change everything.
next: Share the load: agree on specific help with your partner, family or friends.
One 5-minute moment of connection a day: just a hug and eye contact.
If you’ve felt sad or hopeless for more than two weeks, talk to a doctor or psychologist.

styleQuiz.note: This quiz isn’t a diagnosis — it’s a simple tool for self-reflection. It’s based on Baumrind’s dimensions of warmth and structure.

milestoneQuiz.title: What should my child be able to do at this age?
milestoneQuiz.intro: A short check based on the developmental milestones of the CDC and the American Academy of Pediatrics. Most children (about 3 in 4) show these skills at this age. Every child develops at their own pace.
milestoneQuiz.regression: Have they lost a skill they used to have (words, play, movement)?

items.text: Smiles on their own when they see you, tries to get your attention.
items.support: Spend lots of time face to face: smile, wait, respond to their smile.

items.text: Makes sounds like “ah-ah”, “oo-oo”, and makes sounds back when you talk.
items.support: Copy their sounds, then pause so they can “answer”.

items.text: Turns their head towards the sound of your voice.
items.support: Gently call their name from different directions.

items.text: Holds their head steady without support when being held.
items.support: A few short spells of “tummy time” each day while awake.

items.text: Holds on to a toy placed in their hand.
items.support: Give light rattles that are easy to grasp.

items.text: When on their tummy, pushes up on their elbows and lifts their head.
items.support: Put a mirror or a colourful toy in front of them.

items.text: Looks when their name is called.
items.support: Use their name often in games, and smile and praise them when they look.

items.text: Makes different syllables like “ma-ma-ma”, “ba-ba-ba”.
items.support: Repeat syllables together, sing songs.

items.text: Lifts their arms up to be picked up.
items.support: Before picking them up, ask: “Up?” and wait for them to open their arms.

items.text: Looks for things when they drop out of sight.
items.support: Play peekaboo and “where’s the toy?” games.

items.text: Sits without support.
items.support: Give safe floor play time, and protect them with cushions while they sit.

items.text: Is wary of strangers or clings to you.
items.support: This is a sign of attachment. Don’t rush introductions to new people.

items.text: Points to show you something interesting.
items.support: Point and name things yourself: “Look, a bird!” Respond eagerly when they point.

items.text: Says at least 3 words besides “mama” and “dada”.
items.support: Talk your way through everyday tasks and expand on their words.

items.text: Follows a simple instruction without gestures (“give me the ball”).
items.support: Keep instructions short, and thank them happily when they do it.

items.text: Walks without support.
items.support: Give lots of chances to move around barefoot in a safe space.

items.text: Copies you doing chores (sweeping, talking on the phone).
items.support: Give them a little broom or toy dishes, and “do the chores” together.

items.text: Feeds themselves with their fingers, tries to use a spoon.
items.support: Let them get messy and offer finger foods.

items.text: Says about 50 words.
items.support: Read books together, name the pictures, ask open questions.

items.text: Puts two words together, including a verb (“cat runs”).
items.support: Stretch their one word into two: “Car.” — “Big car going!”

items.text: Uses words like “I”, “me”, “we”.
items.support: In turn-taking games, say “my turn, your turn”.

items.text: Plays pretend (feeding a doll, driving a block like a car).
items.support: Join in their pretend play and suggest simple storylines.

items.text: Follows two-step instructions (“pick up the toy and put it in the box”).
items.support: Give instructions as a game, practising one step first, then two.

items.text: Jumps off the ground with both feet.
items.support: Jumping games outdoors, playing “bunnies”.

items.text: Makes sentences of 4 or more words.
items.support: Talk about your day and expand their stories with questions.

items.text: Tells you about something that happened during the day.
items.support: Have a “best moment of the day” chat in the evening.

items.text: Pretends to be someone else in play (a teacher, a superhero).
items.support: Give time and materials for dressing up and pretend play.

items.text: Enjoys playing with other children and comforts them.
items.support: Arrange short playdates and help them name feelings.

items.text: Names a few colours.
items.support: Name colours in everyday life and make a game of it.

items.text: Catches a large ball most of the time, holds a crayon with their fingers.
items.support: Ball games, drawing, play dough.

items.text: Mostly handles daily self-care (getting dressed, brushing teeth) on their own.
items.support: Give age-appropriate independence and support it with picture routines.

items.text: Has at least one friend and enjoys playing with them.
items.support: Make room for friendships, and practise social skills at home.

items.text: Follows the rules of games and can wait for their turn.
items.support: Play board games with rules as a family.

items.text: Can explain their feelings in words.
items.support: Make talking about feelings an everyday habit.

items.text: Reading and counting skills are progressing in line with their school year.
items.support: Stay in touch with the teacher, read together and appreciate their effort.

items.text: Calms down within a reasonable time after getting upset.
items.support: Choose and practise calm-down strategies together.

ontrack.title: Everything is on track
ontrack.short: Your child is showing most of the skills expected at this age.
detail: If you have some “not yet” answers, don’t worry: children pick up some skills a little later and others earlier.
Ask the doctor your questions about development at every check-up — that’s the best way to keep track.

watch.title: A few skills are still developing
watch.short: There are a few “not yet” or “not sure” answers. You can support these skills through everyday play.
detail: Support them with the tips below for 4–6 weeks, then check again.
If you’re still concerned, talk to your paediatrician without waiting for the next check-up. Early support is always better than waiting.

talk.title: We recommend talking to your paediatrician
talk.short: Some answers are signals a doctor should look at. This isn’t a diagnosis, but there’s no need to wait.
detail: Loss of skills (regression) or delays in key milestones call for an early assessment. Support that starts early gives the best results.
You can show this list to the doctor at your appointment.

milestoneQuiz.note: This check isn’t a screening tool or a diagnosis. If you’re concerned, see a doctor whatever the result.

Learn the Signs. Act Early. (inkişaf mərhələləri bələdçisi)

0-1.title: Answer their sounds
0-1.text: When your baby says “ah-ah”, answer back and then wait a moment. This little “conversation” is the first building block of language.

0-1.title: Cuddles don’t spoil
0-1.text: In the early months, responding to crying teaches your baby to trust the world. Hold them, and relax.

0-1.title: Narrate your day
0-1.text: “Now we’re changing your nappy, lifting your legs…” Words are the best toy a baby can have.

0-1.title: 5 minutes face to face
0-1.text: Put the phone aside, look into your baby’s eyes, smile, sing. A few times today.

0-1.title: Play peekaboo
0-1.text: Hide your face behind your hands and say “peekaboo!” Your baby learns that “what goes away comes back”.

0-1.title: When your patience runs out
0-1.text: Put your baby down on their back in the cot and breathe for 5 minutes. That’s the right thing to do. Never shake a baby.

0-1.title: A familiar rhythm
0-1.text: Not an exact clock, but a familiar order: feed, play, sleep. A predictable day calms a baby.

0-1.title: Meet a book
0-1.text: Turn the pages of a board book together and name the pictures. You can read even at this age.

0-1.title: Tummy time
0-1.text: A few short spells on their tummy each day while awake. Put your face in front of them.

0-1.title: Your own rest
0-1.text: Just once while your baby sleeps, skip the housework and rest yourself. Calm parent, calm baby.

0-1.title: A crying plan
0-1.text: Write a plan on paper for the hardest hours: who will help, which techniques you’ll try, what you’ll do when your patience runs out.

0-1.title: A crying diary
0-1.text: For a few days, note when the crying happens and how long it lasts. These notes are very useful when you see the doctor.

0-1.title: Skin to skin
0-1.text: Lay your baby in just a nappy on your chest and cover you both. Your heartbeat and warmth calm them.

0-1.title: A rhythmic sound
0-1.text: A “shhh” sound or quiet humming for a few minutes. It reminds your baby of familiar sounds from the womb.

0-1.title: Back to sleep
0-1.text: For every sleep, put your baby on their back on a flat, firm surface, with no pillow or duvet.

0-1.title: Night shifts
0-1.text: Share the night with your partner: one feeds, the other changes the nappy and settles the baby.

0-1.title: A help list
0-1.text: Who can bring food, who can hold the baby for an hour? Make a list, and when someone asks, name one job.

0-1.title: How are you today?
0-1.text: Rate yourself from 0 to 10. If it’s low for several days, tell someone close and your doctor.

0-1.title: Call them by name
0-1.text: Speak to your baby using their name and smile. At around 9 months they start turning to their name.

0-1.title: No rush with guests
0-1.text: When guests come, let your baby stay in your arms first. When they’re ready, they’ll show interest themselves.

0-1.title: Talk as you leave
0-1.text: When you leave the room, say: “I’m going to the kitchen, I’ll be right back.” Your voice comforts them.

0-1.title: Read the signals
0-1.text: Turning their head away, closing their eyes? Your baby is saying “I need a little break”. Take them somewhere quiet.

0-1.title: If they push the spoon away
0-1.text: Turning their head away at a meal means “I’m full”. Not one more spoonful; calmly finish.

0-1.title: Mess is allowed
0-1.text: First foods are explored with the hands. Put a mat underneath and let them squash, smell and taste.

0-1.title: Dummy rules
0-1.text: Don’t clean the dummy with your own mouth, don’t dip it in sugar, don’t tie it around the neck.

0-1.title: Mirror game
0-1.text: Hold your baby in front of a mirror and pull faces. They look with interest at their own face and your expressions.

0-1.title: A song for transitions
0-1.text: The same short song for each transition: bath, bed, a walk. The song tells them “what happens now”.

0-1.title: Outdoors
0-1.text: A short walk once a day. Daylight and fresh air are good for both your baby and you.

0-1.title: Everything goes in the mouth
0-1.text: Babies put everything in their mouths. Keep small objects, batteries and medicines out of reach.

0-1.title: Good enough
0-1.text: There is no perfect mother. What your baby needs is a sincere parent who can repair.

1-3.title: Give two choices instead of “no”
1-3.text: At this age children want independence. “Red boots or blue?” turns an argument into a game.

1-3.title: Announce the transition
1-3.text: “Two more goes on the slide, then we’re going home.” A warning prevents half of all tantrums.

1-3.title: Name the feeling
1-3.text: “You’re angry because the tower fell down.” A feeling that has a name settles faster.

1-3.title: What can they do?
1-3.text: Instead of “not on the wall”, say “draw on this paper”. Let your child know what to do.

1-3.title: Their game
1-3.text: Today, play for 10 minutes with them in charge: whatever they do, you do too. No barrage of questions.

1-3.title: The hunger tantrum
1-3.text: Notice when tantrums happen. They often coincide with hunger and tiredness. A snack is a secret weapon.

1-3.title: Catch the good
1-3.text: “You tidied your toys all by yourself!” Specific praise makes behaviour grow.

1-3.title: Turn one word into two
1-3.text: When they say “car”, you say “red car going!” That’s how you stretch their language.

1-3.title: Calm brakes
1-3.text: During a tantrum, say little and stay close. Your calm is the “brake” they borrow.

1-3.title: Little helper
1-3.text: Putting out napkins, dropping clothes in the basket. Small jobs give them an “I can do it” feeling.

1-3.title: A goodbye ritual
1-3.text: The same short goodbye every day: a hug, a kiss, “I’ll come after your nap”, and go.

1-3.title: The “wait” game
1-3.text: A small practice: “Let me finish my tea, then I’ll come.” Short waits build patience step by step.

1-3.title: Tidy up with a song
1-3.text: Sing the same song for tidying up toys. Everyone helps until the song ends.

1-3.title: Body names
1-3.text: At bath time, name body parts with their correct names. A calm tone, no shame.

1-3.title: Kisses aren’t compulsory
1-3.text: If they don’t want to kiss a relative, don’t force them. A wave is a hello too.

1-3.title: Give feelings a colour
1-3.text: Let feelings have colours: red anger, blue sadness. Your child can point to a colour and say how they feel.

1-3.title: A small risk
1-3.text: Let them climb in a safe place, and stay close. That’s how the “I can do it” feeling grows.

1-3.title: Kitchen helper
1-3.text: Let them wash vegetables and stir the salad. Children taste what they made themselves more eagerly.

1-3.title: Repeat new foods
1-3.text: Offer a refused food again a few days later, without comment. Acceptance often comes after 8–10 tries.

1-3.title: Let them choose the book
1-3.text: Tonight, let your child choose the book. Read it even if they ask for the same one 20 times: repetition is how they learn.

1-3.title: Taking turns to talk
1-3.text: Listen without interrupting and don’t rush to finish their words. Give your child time to speak.

1-3.title: I make mistakes too
1-3.text: Fix a small mistake of your own out loud: “Hmm, I forgot. Let me do it again.”

1-3.title: One language with grandma
1-3.text: Agree with grandma in advance: safety rules are the same in every home.

1-3.title: Two languages, one love
1-3.text: If there are two languages at home, read and play in each. Mixing languages is normal.

1-3.title: Dummy only for sleep
1-3.text: After the age of 1, gradually keep the dummy only for sleep. Try other ways of calming down during the day.

1-3.title: Changes in advance
1-3.text: A new nursery, a move, a new room? Talk about it with pictures a week or two ahead.

1-3.title: Not a wrong step
1-3.text: If they repeat words and syllables (“ca-ca-car”), listen calmly. It’s common at this age.

1-3.title: Time to move
1-3.text: Set aside outdoor time every day for running, jumping and climbing. An active body sleeps better.

1-3.title: Calm after nursery
1-3.text: When they get home from nursery, a snack and a cuddle first. The flood of questions can come later.

1-3.title: Say it once, show it
1-3.text: Make a request once and show how to do it. Words and actions together are clearer.

3-6.title: Best moment of the day
3-6.text: In the evening ask: “What did you like most today? What was the hardest bit?” And really listen.

3-6.title: Praise the effort
3-6.text: Not “you’re so clever”, but “look how many times you tried again!” Praising effort builds resilience.

3-6.title: Consequence, not punishment
3-6.text: “If you throw the ball indoors, the ball goes in the cupboard.” Keep the consequence linked to the behaviour, and short.

3-6.title: Draw the rules
3-6.text: Draw 3–4 family rules together in pictures and put them up on the wall.

3-6.title: Small steps towards fear
3-6.text: Not running away from fear, but approaching it one small step at a time: “You’re scared, but you can do it.”

3-6.title: Self-control game
3-6.text: “Red light, green light” is great practice for self-control.

3-6.title: Fix mistakes together
3-6.text: “The water spilled. What shall we do?” Looking for a fix teaches more than blaming.

3-6.title: If you shouted, repair it
3-6.text: “I shouted, and that wasn’t OK. I’m sorry.” Repair teaches your child how to recover from mistakes too.

3-6.title: Screen-free table
3-6.text: Today, eat together with no screens. Conversation is the best “side dish”.

3-6.title: Make the truth safe
3-6.text: Don’t ask a question you already know the answer to. “I see the milk got spilled. Come on, let’s wipe it up together.”

3-6.title: My body
3-6.text: Teach the rule “the parts your underwear covers are yours” at a calm moment, briefly and repeatedly.

3-6.title: Good and bad secrets
3-6.text: A surprise is a good secret. A worrying secret where someone says “don’t tell anyone” must always be told to mum.

3-6.title: Trusted adults
3-6.text: Make a list together: who can they talk to when you’re not there? Dad, grandma, their nursery teacher.

3-6.title: A patience game
3-6.text: “Red light, green light” and “Simon says” practise self-control for school.

3-6.title: Getting dressed alone
3-6.text: One skill each morning: buttons, a zip, shoes. Give them time, and don’t do it for them.

3-6.title: A question after the story
3-6.text: After a book, ask: “What would you have done?” It strengthens thinking and speaking.

3-6.title: Separate time for siblings
3-6.text: A few minutes a day that belong to each child alone. Rivalry goes down.

3-6.title: No comparisons
3-6.text: Don’t say “look at your sister”. Compare your child only with their own yesterday.

3-6.title: Off-limits things
3-6.text: Let each child have a few “only mine” toys. For the rest, turns with a timer.

3-6.title: The end of screen time
3-6.text: Agree before the screen: when the timer rings, it ends. Then plan something interesting.

3-6.title: A simple answer about death
3-6.text: Don’t be afraid of the word “died”. “Their body doesn’t work any more, they don’t feel pain” is simple and true.

3-6.title: A moving book
3-6.text: Before a big change, make an illustrated “our moving book” together.

3-6.title: Bedwetting isn’t a fault
3-6.text: Up to the age of 5, wetting at night is often normal. Clean up calmly, don’t scold.

3-6.title: Talk slowly
3-6.text: When your child stutters, don’t say “talk slowly”. Talk slowly and calmly yourself, then listen.

3-6.title: Safe feeling words
3-6.text: Teach harmless words for anger: “I’m going to explode!” Words can replace hitting.

3-6.title: A small job, a big contribution
3-6.text: Setting the table, watering a plant. “You helped the family” is stronger than a reward.

3-6.title: Grandma’s house is different
3-6.text: “At grandma’s it’s like this, and at ours it’s like this.” Different rules don’t confuse a child.

3-6.title: Invite a friend
3-6.text: Invite a friend over and plan a short, simple game. Friendship grows with practice.

3-6.title: Sleep is the best lesson
3-6.text: At 3–6, children need 10–13 hours of sleep a night. An early bedtime is the next day’s mood.

3-6.title: Draw the feeling
3-6.text: After a big feeling, draw a picture of it together. When words can’t be found, colour helps.

6-12.title: Chat without questions
6-12.text: In the car or before bed, tell them about your day without asking questions. Your child will open up too.

6-12.title: Snack first after school
6-12.text: When they come through the door: no questions, just water and a snack. Talk can come later.

6-12.title: Help, don’t do it for them
6-12.text: With homework, don’t give the answer — ask a question: “What do we know here?”

6-12.title: The word “yet”
6-12.text: When your child says “I can’t do it”, add: “…yet.” This little word builds a growth mindset.

6-12.title: Family screen plan
6-12.text: Write the screen rules together: where, when, how much. Children stick to rules more when they helped make them.

6-12.title: One-on-one time
6-12.text: This week, just you and them: a walk, cooking, a game. Let them choose.

6-12.title: Listen to the small things
6-12.text: If you listen to their small problems, they’ll bring you their big ones too.

6-12.title: The value of mistakes
6-12.text: This evening, everyone shares the day’s “most useful mistake”. You go first.

6-12.title: Give responsibility
6-12.text: Packing their own bag, cooking something simple. Real tasks build self-confidence.

6-12.title: Protect sleep
6-12.text: 9–12 hours of sleep matters as much as lessons. Phones stay out of the bedroom at night.

6-12.title: Four online rules
6-12.text: Name, address, school and photos aren’t given to strangers; no going to meet someone alone; passwords only with a parent; if something bothers you, come to me.

6-12.title: I won’t take your phone
6-12.text: Promise: “If you tell me about something that bothers you, I won’t take your device away.” Your child will keep talking to you.

6-12.title: Learn their game
6-12.text: Watch your child’s favourite game or channel together for 15 minutes. Ask with curiosity, don’t judge.

6-12.title: Pocket money day
6-12.text: Choose a fixed day and a small amount. Let your child divide it into “spend, save, share” boxes themselves.

6-12.title: When the money runs out
6-12.text: When pocket money runs out, don’t give more. Calmly ask: “What would you do next time?”

6-12.title: A savings picture
6-12.text: Draw a picture of something big they want and mark together each week how much is left.

6-12.title: Body and online
6-12.text: Nobody should ask for photos or say “it’s our secret”. Remind them of this at a calm moment.

6-12.title: Patience with stuttering
6-12.text: Don’t rush to finish their words; look them in the eyes and wait. Answer slowly and calmly.

6-12.title: A plan for bedwetting
6-12.text: If it continues after the age of 6, talk to a doctor without shaming. Effective treatments exist.

6-12.title: Honest about loss
6-12.text: Answer their questions honestly. “I don’t know, but let’s think about it together” is a good answer too.

6-12.title: The strength of the wider family
6-12.text: Plan time together with the grandparents. Family stories give a child roots and strength.

6-12.title: The value of two languages
6-12.text: Keep the home language alive with books, letters and family stories. Don’t let the school language crowd it out.

6-12.title: No messengers in a separation
6-12.text: If the parents live apart, don’t make your child carry messages. Grown-up matters stay with the grown-ups.

6-12.title: What stays the same
6-12.text: With a move or a new school, make a “what doesn’t change” list: family evening, rituals, calls with friends.

6-12.title: Observe and write it down
6-12.text: If you have concerns about attention or communication, write down specific examples and take them to the doctor.

6-12.title: A sibling meeting
6-12.text: A short family meeting once a week: what went well, which rule shall we change?

6-12.title: Cook together
6-12.text: Once a week, cook a simple meal together: measuring, reading, planning, all in one.

6-12.title: Give real choices
6-12.text: Which club, which book, what shall we do on Saturday? Making choices teaches responsibility.

6-12.title: Be a good listener
6-12.text: Today when your child talks, don’t interrupt or give advice; just ask: “What happened next?”

6-12.title: Mistakes are lessons too
6-12.text: When your child makes a mistake, let your first words be “Let’s see what we learned”, not a telling-off.
